stimuli.title: Case study: warehouse system replacement
stimuli.text:
You are the project manager for Northgate Logistics, which is replacing the warehouse management system at its three regional distribution centers. The project has two tracks. The facilities track (new scanners, network cabling and racking changes) is planned predictively with a baselined schedule and a fixed-price contract with an installer. The software track uses two agile teams working in two-week sprints with a product owner from the operations department.

The sponsor is the VP of Operations. Shift supervisors at the largest site were not interviewed during planning and have told their teams that the new system will slow picking down. The installer has reported that one of its two certified technicians is leaving the company next month.

Status at the end of month 6 (facilities track):

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Budget at completion (BAC) | \$800,000 |
| Planned value (PV) | \$400,000 |
| Earned value (EV) | \$360,000 |
| Actual cost (AC) | \$450,000 |

stimuli.title: Case study: smart water meter rollout
stimuli.text:
You are the project manager for a city water utility that is replacing 40,000 mechanical meters with smart meters and launching a customer app that shows daily water use. Meter installation is planned predictively in four geographic phases and is done by a contractor under a fixed-price contract. The app is built by an internal agile team that releases every two weeks.

The project reports monthly to a steering committee chaired by the utility's general manager, and quarterly to the city council. The utility has a sustainability target of cutting water loss by 15 percent, and the business case depends on leak alerts in the app. The national privacy regulator has just published draft guidance on how utilities may store hourly usage data.

Status at the end of phase 2 (installation track):

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Budget at completion (BAC) | \$2,000,000 |
| Planned value (PV) | \$1,000,000 |
| Earned value (EV) | \$800,000 |
| Actual cost (AC) | \$800,000 |

questions.stem: Read the case study. What is the best way to deal with the shift supervisors at the largest site?
options: Delay go-live at the largest site until the supervisors stop telling their teams that picking will slow
Send the supervisors the business case so that they can see the productivity gains the system will bring
Meet with the supervisors to hear their concerns and involve them in testing the new picking workflows
Ask the VP of Operations to tell the supervisors that the decision is final and they must support it
questions.explanation: The supervisors were missed during stakeholder analysis and now influence many users. Engaging them, hearing their concerns and involving them in testing builds ownership and may reveal real workflow problems. Using authority, sending documents or simply waiting does not address their concerns.

questions.stem: Read the case study. Which reason best supports using a predictive approach for the facilities track and an agile approach for the software track?
options: Predictive approaches are always cheaper for hardware, while agile approaches always deliver software faster than predictive ones
The installer's fixed-price contract forbids agile methods, while the software teams have no contract and can work as they like
Using two approaches lets the project report earned value for the facilities track and avoid reporting on the software at all
The facilities work has stable, well-defined requirements, while the warehouse software needs will be refined through user feedback
questions.explanation: Tailoring the approach to each part of the work is the point of hybrid delivery: stable, costly-to-change physical work suits predictive planning, and software whose needs emerge with use suits iteration. The other options are overgeneralizations or misread the purpose of the choice.

questions.stem: Read the case study. What is the cost performance index (CPI) of the facilities track at the end of month 6? Round to two decimal places. Type the number only.
questions.explanation: CPI = EV / AC = 360,000 / 450,000 = 0.80. The track is getting 80 cents of planned value for every dollar spent, so it is over budget. (SPI = EV / PV = 360,000 / 400,000 = 0.90, so it is also behind schedule.)

questions.stem: Read the case study. The VP of Operations asks you to add a fourth distribution center, which is still under construction, to the facilities track now. What should you do?
options: Decline the request, since the facilities track is predictive and its baselined scope cannot change
Analyze the request's effect on the facilities baseline and contract, then take it through change control
Ask the installer to include the fourth site within the existing fixed price, since the scope is similar
Add the fourth site to the schedule, since the VP of Operations is the sponsor and can authorize the work
questions.explanation: A change to baselined scope that also affects a fixed-price contract needs impact analysis and change control, even when the sponsor asks. Adding it directly bypasses the process, expecting the installer to absorb new scope ignores the contract, and predictive scope can change through the proper process.

questions.stem: Read the case study. What is the best way to handle the news that one of the installer's two certified technicians is leaving?
options: Record it as a risk, assess its effect on the installation schedule and agree a response with the installer
Have your own warehouse staff take over the network cabling work so that the technician is not needed
Do nothing, since staffing the work is entirely the installer's problem under a fixed-price contract
Ask the installer to pay a penalty now, because the technician's departure will delay the installation
questions.explanation: The departure is a threat to the facilities schedule; it should be analyzed and a response agreed with the seller (for example, a replacement technician or adjusted sequencing). Even with a fixed price, delays hurt the buyer's project, a penalty before any breach is premature, and untrained staff doing certified work creates new risk.

questions.stem: During a daily stand-up, two senior developers start arguing about which database design to use. The argument is getting personal and the rest of the team is uncomfortable. What should you do first?
options: Report the behavior to both developers' functional managers so they can address it as a conduct issue
Ask the solution architect to choose one design so the argument ends before it affects the sprint
Postpone the topic until the next retrospective so that the current sprint is not disrupted by the argument
Move the debate out of the stand-up, then meet both developers to understand and resolve it together
questions.explanation: Collaborating (problem solving) addresses the root of the conflict and keeps the relationship intact, and moving it out of the stand-up keeps that meeting short. Forcing a decision through the architect ends the argument but not the disagreement, delaying it to the retrospective is withdrawal, and escalating to managers comes only after the project manager has tried to resolve it.

questions.stem: The project charter has just been approved and you have been assigned as project manager. Which should you do next?
options: Ask the sponsor to approve the detailed cost estimates for all work packages
Identify the stakeholders and record them in a stakeholder register
Baseline the schedule and send it to the functional managers for resources
Hold a lessons learned session with the managers of earlier projects
questions.explanation: Identifying stakeholders starts as soon as the charter is approved, because their needs shape every plan that follows. A baseline and detailed cost approval come after planning, and reviewing past lessons helps but does not replace knowing who the stakeholders are.

questions.stem: How does a contingency reserve differ from a management reserve?
options: Contingency covers unknown risks and needs sponsor approval; management reserve covers identified risks and sits inside the cost baseline
Contingency is used only for schedule delays, while management reserve is used only for cost overruns on procurement contracts
Contingency covers identified risks inside the cost baseline; management reserve covers unknown risks and needs management approval to use
There is no real difference, because both are added to the cost baseline and the project manager can spend either one freely
questions.explanation: Contingency reserves are for known risks (known unknowns), are part of the cost baseline and are managed by the project manager. Management reserves are for unforeseen work (unknown unknowns), sit outside the baseline in the total budget and need management approval.

questions.stem: On a predictive project, a stakeholder asks for a change to a design that has already been approved and baselined. What should you do first?
options: Ask the sponsor to approve the change before anyone analyzes it
Make the change, since the stakeholder is entitled to request it
Assess the impact of the change on scope, schedule, cost and risk
Refuse the change, because the approved design has now been baselined
questions.explanation: In integrated change control, the project manager first evaluates the impact so the change control board can make an informed decision. Making or refusing the change without analysis, or seeking approval before analysis, bypasses the process.

questions.stem: A client wants a new mobile app but cannot describe all its features yet, expects its needs to change as it sees early versions, and has a product manager available every week. Which development approach fits best?
options: An adaptive approach with short iterations and frequent customer feedback
A predictive approach with a fixed scope baseline and phase-gate reviews
A predictive approach with all requirements signed off before any design begins
A waterfall approach with a single delivery once all of the features are built
questions.explanation: Unclear and changing requirements plus an available customer are the classic conditions for an adaptive approach. Predictive and single-delivery approaches assume requirements can be fixed early, which this client cannot do.

questions.stem: You are buying a standard software installation service. The scope is fully defined, and your organization wants the seller to carry the risk of cost overruns. Which contract type fits best?
options: Time and materials
Firm fixed price
Cost plus fixed fee
Cost plus percentage of cost
questions.explanation: A firm fixed price contract puts cost risk on the seller and works well when scope is clearly defined. Cost-reimbursable contracts and time and materials contracts leave most of the cost risk with the buyer.

questions.stem: Your agile team has been waiting a week for another department to set up a test environment, and stories are piling up as not done. What should you do?
options: Ask the team to start new stories so that their time is not wasted during the wait
Wait for the other department, since setting up environments is not the team's job
Work with the other department to remove the blocker, and keep it visible to the team
Mark the stories as done, since the code is finished and only testing is outstanding
questions.explanation: Removing impediments is a core servant leadership duty: the project manager engages the blocking party and makes the impediment visible. Starting more work raises work in progress, waiting passively lets the block persist, and stories are not done until they meet the definition of done.

questions.stem: You are forming a hybrid team with members in three countries. In the first two weeks, meetings start late, people talk over each other and some members never speak. What is the best action?
options: Keep a log of who arrives late or interrupts others and share it with each member's manager at month end
Facilitate a session where the team agrees its own ground rules and records them in a team charter
Publish a list of meeting rules yourself and remind members of them at the start of every meeting
Ask human resources to schedule cultural awareness training for the team before the next phase
questions.explanation: Ground rules that the team writes itself in a team charter get far more buy-in than rules handed down. Training may help later but does not fix the immediate working norms, and logging behavior for managers damages trust.

questions.stem: Using a power/interest grid, select the engagement approach for each stakeholder.
rows: The sponsor, who controls the budget and reviews progress every week
A regional director who can stop the project but rarely shows interest in it
Warehouse staff who will use the system daily but cannot change project decisions
A department that is barely affected and has little influence on the project
questions.explanation: High power and high interest: manage closely. High power, low interest: keep satisfied. Low power, high interest: keep informed. Low power, low interest: monitor with minimal effort.

questions.stem: A project has a budget at completion of \$300,000 and a cost performance index of 0.75. Assuming current cost performance continues, what is the estimate at completion? Type the number only, with no commas or currency sign.
questions.explanation: EAC = BAC / CPI = 300,000 / 0.75 = 400,000. When performance to date is expected to continue, dividing the budget by the CPI gives the forecast total cost.

questions.stem: The change control board has approved a change that adds a reporting module. What should you do next?
options: Update the affected plans and baselines, then implement and communicate the change
Send the change back to the stakeholder who requested it, for a second approval
Add the change to the issue log and wait for the sponsor to say when to begin
Implement the change at once and update the plans at the end of the current phase
questions.explanation: Once approved, a change is reflected in the project management plan and baselines, implemented, and communicated to stakeholders. Delaying the updates makes the baseline wrong, and the approval has already been given.

questions.stem: Your project is to build a pedestrian bridge. The design has been approved by the city, the requirements are set by building codes and changes after construction starts are very expensive. Which approach fits best?
options: A predictive approach with a detailed plan and baselines
An adaptive approach with two-week sprints and a backlog
A kanban approach with no plan beyond the current work items
An iterative approach that rebuilds the bridge in versions
questions.explanation: Stable, well-defined requirements and a high cost of change favor a predictive approach. Iterating on a physical bridge or working without a plan is impractical and unsafe.

questions.stem: You need a specialist to start next week to help diagnose an unknown performance problem. Nobody knows yet how much work it will take. Which contract type fits best?
options: Fixed price with incentive fee
Firm fixed price
Time and materials
Fixed price with economic price adjustment
questions.explanation: Time and materials contracts suit small, urgent work whose scope cannot yet be defined; a not-to-exceed limit can cap the buyer's exposure. Fixed-price contracts need a defined scope, which this work does not have.

questions.stem: Your team agreed that every code change needs a peer review before merging. One developer has merged changes without review three times this sprint. What should you do?
options: Ask the developer's functional manager to add a note about the unreviewed merges to the next performance review
Speak privately with the developer about the agreed rule and the impact the skipped reviews are having
Raise it at the next retrospective and ask the developer to explain the merges in front of the team
Ask the tools administrator to remove the developer's permission to merge into the main branch
questions.explanation: Managing a ground rule violation starts with a private, respectful conversation about the agreement and its impact. Public questioning embarrasses the person, and removing permissions or involving the functional manager are steps for when a direct conversation has failed.

questions.stem: A department head is openly resisting your agile project and has told her staff not to attend the story-writing workshops. What should you do first?
options: Hold the workshops without her department and record the decision in the issue log
Meet with the department head to understand the concerns behind her resistance
Escalate the resistance to the steering committee as a risk that the project cannot control
Ask the sponsor to instruct the department head to send her staff to the workshops
questions.explanation: Engaging a resistant stakeholder starts with understanding her concerns; there may be a legitimate issue the project should address. Using the sponsor's authority or escalating comes later, and leaving her department out risks requirements that her staff will later reject.

questions.stem: Who should take part in identifying project risks?
options: The project manager alone, during the initial planning phase
The sponsor alone, during each of the phase gate reviews
The team and key stakeholders, throughout the whole project
The risk manager alone, once the project charter is approved
questions.explanation: Risk identification draws on the knowledge of the team and stakeholders and repeats throughout the project as conditions change. Leaving it to one person or one moment misses many risks.

questions.stem: For a task, the team gives an optimistic estimate of 4 days, a most likely estimate of 7 days and a pessimistic estimate of 16 days. What is the beta (PERT) estimate in days? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: Beta (PERT) estimate = (O + 4M + P) / 6 = (4 + 28 + 16) / 6 = 48 / 6 = 8 days. The weighting toward the most likely value is offset here by the long pessimistic tail.

questions.stem: On a hybrid project, the agile team wants to add a feature that would push the date of a contractual milestone on the predictive track. What should you do?
options: Assess the effect on the milestone and take the request through the integrated change process
Reject the feature outright, since contractual milestones on the predictive track cannot move
Let the product owner add the feature to the backlog, since backlog changes need no approval
Have the team build the feature quietly and try to recover the lost time in later sprints
questions.explanation: Backlog changes inside the agile track are the product owner's call, but once a change affects a baselined, contractual milestone it needs the integrated change process. Treating it as a backlog-only decision, rejecting it outright or hiding it are all wrong.

questions.stem: What is the lowest level of a work breakdown structure called?
options: Activity in the schedule
Project deliverable
Work package
Control account
questions.explanation: The work package is the lowest level of the WBS, where cost and duration can be estimated and managed. Activities are decomposed from work packages in schedule planning, and control accounts sit above work packages for management control.

questions.stem: Your agile team is made up of experienced specialists who are used to organizing their own work. Which leadership approach best fits this team?
options: Laissez-faire leadership: stay out of the team's work entirely, including its impediments and any stakeholder requests
Servant leadership: remove impediments, shield the team from distractions and let members decide how to do the work
Directive leadership: assign daily tasks to each specialist and check progress at the end of every day
Transactional leadership: set individual targets and tie rewards closely to each person's output
questions.explanation: A skilled, self-organizing team needs a servant leader who removes obstacles and protects its focus. Directive and transactional styles undercut self-organization, and laissez-faire abandons the team when it needs help with blockers and stakeholders.

questions.stem: You want a simple tool that compares each stakeholder's current level of engagement with the level the project needs. Which tool should you use?
options: Stakeholder engagement assessment matrix
Probability and impact matrix
Responsibility assignment matrix for the project team
Requirements traceability matrix
questions.explanation: The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix records current (C) and desired (D) engagement, such as unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive or leading, which shows where engagement work is needed. The other matrices cover roles, requirements and risks.

questions.stem: For each contract, select which party carries most of the cost risk.
rows: Firm fixed price contract
Cost plus fixed fee contract
Cost plus percentage of cost contract
Purchase order at a catalogue price
questions.explanation: In fixed-price arrangements, including a purchase order at a set price, the seller absorbs overruns. In cost-reimbursable contracts the buyer pays the seller's actual costs, so the buyer carries the risk; cost plus percentage of cost is the worst case for the buyer because the fee grows with cost.

questions.stem: An activity on the critical path will finish 3 days late. If nothing else changes, what is the effect on the project?
options: The non-critical activities absorb the delay
The project finish date does not change
The project finish date moves 3 days later
Only the activity's own float is used up
questions.explanation: Activities on the critical path have zero total float, so any delay to them delays the project finish by the same amount unless the schedule is compressed.

questions.stem: A requested change would add 12 percent to the project budget. The governance plan allows you to approve changes of up to 5 percent. What should you do?
options: Approve the change, since you are accountable for delivering the project within its budget
Reject the change, since it is above your limit and therefore cannot be approved by anyone
Split the change into three smaller changes so that each one falls within your approval limit
Analyze the change and escalate it through the governance path set for changes of this size
questions.explanation: Governance sets escalation paths and thresholds; changes above the project manager's authority go to the body the plan names, with analysis attached. Approving beyond authority or splitting the change to avoid the threshold breaches governance, and outright rejection ignores the escalation path.

questions.stem: Your team has finished a deliverable, and quality control has verified that it meets the specifications. What is the next step?
options: Have the customer or sponsor review and formally accept the deliverable
Archive the deliverable and close the work package in the WBS dictionary
Run a lessons learned session on the deliverable before anyone reviews it
Hand the deliverable to operations, since quality control has passed it
questions.explanation: Verified deliverables go to validate scope, where the customer or sponsor formally accepts them. Quality control checks correctness; acceptance is a separate step that must happen before handover or closure.

questions.stem: Halfway through a project, you notice that team members describe the project's goal in noticeably different ways, and some are building features that no stakeholder asked for. What should you do first?
options: Find out where the understanding diverged, then revisit the vision with the team and key stakeholders
Ask each team member to reread the project charter and confirm by email that they understand it
Ask the sponsor to send the whole team a message restating the project's goals and its expected business benefits
Rewrite the scope statement in more detail and send it to every team member with a read receipt
questions.explanation: A misunderstanding of the vision should be broken down to its root cause, then the vision is revisited with the people who own it so it is shared, not just restated. Sending documents or messages repeats the words without checking or rebuilding understanding.

questions.stem: Select the threat response strategy shown by each action.
rows: Buy insurance against damage to equipment in transit
Redesign the product to remove a part from an unreliable supplier
Qualify a second supplier for a critical component
Set aside a contingency reserve and monitor the risk
questions.explanation: Insurance transfers the financial impact to a third party. Removing the part eliminates the threat (avoid). A second supplier reduces its probability and impact (mitigate). A reserve with monitoring is active acceptance.

questions.stem: Your project team is growing from 8 people to 12 people. How many additional communication channels will this create? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: Channels = n(n - 1) / 2. Eight people have 8 x 7 / 2 = 28 channels; twelve have 12 x 11 / 2 = 66. The increase is 66 - 28 = 38, which is why adding people adds communication effort quickly.

questions.stem: A non-critical activity has 5 days of total float. It is delayed by 3 days. What is the effect?
options: The finish date moves 3 days later, because every delay affects the end date
The finish date moves 2 days later, because float covers only part of the delay
The activity becomes critical, and the finish date moves 5 days later
The finish date does not change, and the activity has 2 days of float left
questions.explanation: Total float is how long an activity can slip without delaying the project finish. A 3-day delay against 5 days of float uses 3 days and leaves 2; the end date is unaffected.

questions.stem: You are starting a hybrid project in an organization that has a PMO with policies, templates and historical records. How should you use them?
options: Use them only if the sponsor asks you to follow the PMO's standards
Use the organization's process assets and tailor them to the project
Ignore them and design new processes that fit this project's needs
Use every template exactly as it is written, whatever the project's size
questions.explanation: Organizational process assets (policies, procedures, templates, lessons learned) give a starting point and are tailored to the project. Ignoring them wastes knowledge, rigid use can add needless overhead, and they apply regardless of whether the sponsor mentions them.

questions.stem: A supplier of hardware for your hybrid project has delivered three shipments late, and the contract includes delivery performance terms. What should you do first?
options: Increase the order quantities so the late deliveries have less impact on the project schedule
Review the supplier's performance against the contract terms and meet to agree corrective action
Terminate the contract for default and start a new procurement process with a different supplier
Withhold all payments to the supplier until it has delivered three shipments on time in a row
questions.explanation: Managing a supplier starts with assessing performance against the contract and working with the supplier on corrective action, using the remedies the contract provides if needed. Termination and withholding payment are escalations that may breach the contract if used first.

questions.stem: During backlog refinement, the team asks you how to split a large user story into smaller ones. What is the best response?
options: Split the story yourself after the meeting and add the smaller stories to the backlog for the team
Ask the agile coach to take over backlog refinement until the team has more experience splitting stories
Encourage the team to decide how to split it, and offer a few splitting techniques if they want them
Ask the product owner to split the story on their own and assign the smaller stories to members
questions.explanation: Empowering the team means letting it own how the work is broken down, with the project manager supporting rather than deciding. The product owner collaborates on splitting but does not do it alone or assign work, and handing refinement to someone else removes the team's learning.

questions.stem: During a review of the work, you find that a developer added a reporting feature that the customer mentioned informally in a hallway conversation. It is not in the scope baseline. What should you do?
options: Remind the developer that scope changes follow the agreed process, and assess the feature's impact
Keep the feature, since the customer asked for it and the developer has already finished the work
Add the feature to the scope baseline yourself, since the work has already been completed and tested
Remove the feature immediately and say nothing to the customer, so as to avoid raising expectations
questions.explanation: This is scope creep, and the feature has impacts on testing, cost and support. The project manager reinforces the process and evaluates the impact so a proper decision can be made. Keeping it, silently removing it or updating the baseline without change control all bypass the process.

questions.stem: Executives say your status reports are too long, while the delivery teams say the same reports leave out details they need. What should you do?
options: Shorten the report for everyone and ask team members to find missing details on their own
Replace the written reports with one weekly meeting that every stakeholder group must attend
Keep a single report for everyone, so that no stakeholder group ever misses any information
Tailor the reporting: a one-page summary for executives and detailed reports for the teams
questions.explanation: Communication should be tailored to each audience's needs: decision-level summaries for executives, working detail for teams. A single report satisfies neither group, a mandatory all-hands meeting wastes time, and shortening for everyone leaves the teams short of information.

questions.stem: You must shorten the schedule by two weeks. The sponsor has approved extra budget, but the activities are tightly dependent, and overlapping them would cause rework. Which technique should you use?
options: Resource leveling across all activities on the schedule
Crashing critical path activities by adding resources
Adding lag between each pair of dependent activities
Fast tracking critical activities so they run in parallel
questions.explanation: Crashing adds resources (cost) to shorten critical path activities, which fits when budget is available and overlapping is risky. Fast tracking would cause the rework described, resource leveling usually lengthens the schedule, and lag adds time.

questions.stem: At the start of a project to launch a customer self-service portal, what should you do about success measures?
options: Let each stakeholder decide at closure whether the project succeeded
Use on-time and on-budget delivery as the only criteria for success
Define success criteria after the first release, once data is available
Agree measurable success criteria with the sponsor and key stakeholders
questions.explanation: Success metrics are defined early and agreed with the people who judge success, and they usually include outcomes and value (for example call volume reduction), not just time and budget. Deciding at closure or after release leaves the team without a target.

questions.stem: A new team member works eight hours ahead of the rest of the team and says they feel left out of decisions. Which TWO actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Rotate recurring meeting times so the inconvenience of early or late calls is shared
Ask the member to work the main office's hours so they can join every discussion
Excuse the member from team meetings and send them the meeting notes instead
Pair the new member with an experienced teammate who can act as a buddy
Assign the member only independent tasks that need little collaboration
questions.explanation: Sharing the burden of meeting times and giving the person a buddy both build inclusion and connection. Sending notes instead of including them, demanding they work night hours, or isolating their work all make the feeling of exclusion worse.

questions.stem: Your risk register lists a threat with a 30 percent chance of costing \$50,000 and an opportunity with a 20 percent chance of saving \$20,000. What is their combined expected monetary value? Type the number only, with no commas or currency sign, and use a minus sign for a net cost.
questions.explanation: EMV = probability x impact, with threats negative and opportunities positive. Threat: 0.30 x -50,000 = -15,000. Opportunity: 0.20 x 20,000 = 4,000. Combined: -15,000 + 4,000 = -11,000.

questions.stem: Which of these is a cost of conformance?
options: Warranty claims from customers after release
Rework on components that failed inspection
Scrapped parts that did not meet specification
Training team members on the coding standard
questions.explanation: Costs of conformance are spent to prevent or detect failures, such as training and inspections. Rework, warranty claims and scrap are costs of nonconformance (failure costs).

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a minimum viable product (MVP)?
options: The smallest release that delivers value and lets the team learn from real users
A prototype for internal testing only, which is thrown away before any real release
A version of the product with the lowest possible quality to save time and cost
The first release, which must contain every feature the customer has asked for
questions.explanation: An MVP is the smallest product that delivers value and validates assumptions with real users, so later work is based on evidence. It is not a throwaway prototype, a complete product, or a low-quality release.

questions.stem: Stakeholders keep interrupting your agile team to ask about progress. What is the best way to reduce these interruptions?
options: Ask stakeholders to send all questions to the product owner in a weekly email
Keep a visible task board and burndown chart that anyone can check at any time
Send the stakeholders a detailed written report of every task at the end of each day
Tell the team to decline every question from stakeholders until the sprint ends
questions.explanation: Information radiators make progress visible without interrupting the team. Weekly emails slow the flow of information, refusing all questions harms relationships, and daily detailed reports add overhead the team does not need.

questions.stem: On your hybrid project, a vendor test data set was not delivered because two team members each believed the other was responsible for it. What is the best way to prevent this from happening again?
options: Add a weekly status meeting where each team member reads out everything they worked on during that week
Work with the team to build a responsibility assignment matrix for the remaining deliverables
Assign every remaining deliverable to yourself so that there is one point of accountability
Ask both team members to write an explanation of the missed deliverable for the project file
questions.explanation: A RACI or other responsibility assignment matrix makes each deliverable's owner explicit, which is exactly what was missing. Written explanations assign blame, taking every deliverable yourself does not scale, and longer status meetings do not clarify ownership.

questions.stem: Your project has a schedule performance index of 0.8 and a cost performance index of 1.1. What is the project's status?
options: Ahead of schedule and under budget
Behind schedule and under budget
Behind schedule and over budget
Ahead of schedule and over budget
questions.explanation: An index below 1.0 is unfavorable and above 1.0 is favorable. SPI 0.8 means only 80 percent of the planned work has been done (behind schedule), and CPI 1.1 means the work done cost less than its value (under budget).

questions.stem: During requirements work, you learn that the new system will store customers' personal data, which is subject to data protection law. What should you do?
options: Leave it to the IT security team to handle after the system goes live in production
Confirm the requirements with the data protection officer and build them into the plan
Record it as a low risk, since the company has never been fined for a data breach
Ask the developers to research the data protection law in their own spare time this month
questions.explanation: Compliance requirements are confirmed with the right experts and built into requirements, design and the plan from the start. Leaving it until after go-live or to informal research risks noncompliance, and past luck is not a basis for risk ratings.

questions.stem: The only engineer who understands the legacy billing interface will leave the company in three weeks. The interface must be changed in the next release. What should you do?
options: Plan to hire an external specialist after the engineer leaves to rebuild the missing knowledge
Ask human resources to delay the engineer's departure date until the next release has gone live
Have the engineer pair with team members and document the critical knowledge before leaving
Capture the engineer's knowledge in the lessons learned session planned for project closure
questions.explanation: The knowledge is critical and leaving soon, so the project manager arranges transfer now through pairing and documentation. Delaying a resignation is usually not possible, rebuilding later costs time, and lessons learned at closure is far too late.

questions.stem: What should a product owner mainly use to order the product backlog?
options: The seniority of the stakeholder who asked for each item, highest first
The order in which stakeholders submitted the requests to the team
Which items the developers find most interesting to work on next
Business value, risk and dependencies, informed by stakeholder feedback
questions.explanation: Backlog ordering maximizes value delivered while managing risk and dependencies, using stakeholder feedback. Submission order, developer preference or requester seniority do not reflect value.

questions.stem: Over the last ten sprints, your agile team has logged 400 defects in 12 categories and wants to focus improvement work where it will have the most effect. Which tool should it use?
options: A Pareto chart
A control chart
A flowchart of the process
A scatter diagram
questions.explanation: A Pareto chart ranks categories by frequency, showing the vital few causes behind most defects. A control chart shows process stability over time, a scatter diagram shows the relation between two variables and a flowchart maps the process.

questions.stem: A risk in your register has now occurred. What should you do?
options: Carry out the planned risk response and record the issue in the issue log
Wait for the next risk review meeting before deciding what action to take
Add the event to the risk register as a new risk and analyze its probability
Escalate the event to the sponsor, since every occurred risk needs a sponsor
questions.explanation: When a risk occurs it becomes an issue: the owner carries out the planned response, and the issue is logged and tracked. It is no longer uncertain, so analyzing probability is pointless, and waiting or escalating by default delays the planned action.

questions.stem: For each situation, select the conflict resolution technique being used.
rows: Each side gives up part of what it wanted so the two can reach a deal
The project manager stresses points of agreement and plays down the differences
The project manager imposes a decision because a safety deadline cannot wait
The parties examine the data together and reach a solution both fully support
questions.explanation: Compromise means both sides give something up, smoothing (accommodating) emphasizes agreement over differences, forcing imposes one view and is justified mainly in emergencies such as safety, and collaborating (problem solving) works through the data to a solution everyone supports.

questions.stem: Halfway through a sprint, the burndown chart shows the remaining work line well above the ideal line. What does this indicate?
options: The sprint has had work removed from it since sprint planning
The team's velocity is higher than it was in previous sprints
The team is ahead of plan and can take on more work this sprint
The team is behind the pace needed to finish the planned work
questions.explanation: On a burndown chart, remaining work above the ideal line means less work has been completed than planned at this point. Being ahead would show the line below the ideal, and removed work would bring the line down.

questions.stem: To save four days, a team lead suggests skipping a mandatory electrical safety inspection before the equipment is energized. What should you do?
options: Keep the inspection in the plan and look for time savings elsewhere
Skip the inspection this once and carry it out after the equipment runs
Skip the inspection if the equipment vendor confirms it is safe to do so
Let the team lead decide, since the team lead is closest to the work
questions.explanation: Mandatory safety and regulatory requirements are not traded for schedule. The consequences of noncompliance (injury, legal action, rework) far outweigh four days, so the project manager finds savings elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which TWO practices help knowledge flow across an agile team? (Choose two.)
options: Limiting wiki editing rights to team leads
Retrospectives with recorded actions
One specialist owning each technical area
Collecting lessons only at project closure
Pairing team members on tasks
questions.explanation: Pairing spreads skills between people, and retrospectives turn experience into shared improvements during the project. Single owners per area create knowledge silos, lessons captured only at closure cannot help this project, and restricted editing discourages sharing.

questions.stem: A project is expected to cut customer onboarding time by 30 percent. The product will be released next month. What should you verify now?
options: That a way to measure the benefit is in place, with a baseline and an owner
That the project team will stay together to measure the benefit for a year
That the sponsor will sign the acceptance form on the day of the release
That the onboarding staff have been told the 30 percent target is now fixed
questions.explanation: Benefits often appear after the project ends, so the project verifies that a measurement system exists: a baseline to compare with, a method and an owner in the business. The project team usually disbands, acceptance does not measure benefits, and announcing the target does not measure anything.

questions.stem: In retrospectives your team rarely raises problems, even though you can see several issues slowing them down. What should you do?
options: Require each team member to bring at least two problems to every retrospective from now on
Invite the sponsor to the next retrospective so that the team can see how much senior leadership values the event
Build psychological safety, for example by changing the retrospective format and being open about your own mistakes
Cancel retrospectives for a while because they are not producing improvement actions
questions.explanation: People raise problems when they feel safe doing so; varying the format (anonymous input, small groups) and modeling openness build that safety. Quotas feel like a test, a senior visitor usually makes people more guarded, and dropping retrospectives removes the improvement loop.

questions.stem: On a control chart, seven measurements in a row fall above the mean, although all are within the control limits. What should you do?
options: Investigate the process for a special cause
Take no action, since no point is out of limits
Stop production until every point is at the mean
Widen the control limits to fit the new data
questions.explanation: Seven or more consecutive points on one side of the mean (the rule of seven) is a non-random pattern that suggests a special cause, even within limits. Ignoring it misses the signal, widening the limits hides it, and stopping all production is an overreaction.

questions.stem: The remaining product backlog for a release is estimated at 240 story points. The team's average velocity is 30 points per sprint. How many sprints should the release take? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: Sprints needed = remaining points / velocity = 240 / 30 = 8. In practice the team would give a range and update it as velocity and the backlog change.

questions.stem: You are planning a hybrid project that is similar to several the organization has run before. What should you do early in planning?
options: Ask the team to avoid the people who ran the old projects
Review the lessons learned from the similar past projects
Copy the schedule of the last project without any change
Wait for lessons to emerge as this project goes forward
questions.explanation: Lessons learned from similar projects are a key organizational asset for planning, risks and estimates. Copying an old schedule ignores differences, waiting wastes known lessons, and the people from past projects are a valuable source of insight.

questions.stem: After a product demonstration, the customer's satisfaction score dropped sharply, although the team delivered every item in the sprint goal. What should you do first?
options: Ask the team to add more features to the next sprint so that the score recovers
Meet with the customer to learn which expectations the increment did not meet
Point out to the customer that every item in the agreed sprint goal was delivered
Report the low score to the sponsor and ask for help in managing the customer's views
questions.explanation: A drop in satisfaction means an expectation gap; the first step is to understand it. Defending the sprint goal does not close the gap, adding features may miss the real concern, and escalating before understanding the cause is premature.

questions.stem: On a hybrid project, who should own a risk in the risk register?
options: The project manager, who should own every risk in the register
The sponsor, because the sponsor is accountable for the project
The person best placed to monitor the risk and carry out its response
The team member who first raised the risk during identification
questions.explanation: Each risk is assigned to the person best able to watch its triggers and carry out the response. The project manager oversees the process but cannot own every risk, and the person who raised it may not be the right owner.

questions.stem: Your team's velocity has fallen for three sprints. A team member tells you that production support tickets are taking up a growing share of their day. What should you do?
options: Raise the velocity target for the next sprint so the team has a clear goal to work toward
Make the support work visible and agree with the team and product owner how much capacity it should get
Report the velocity decline to the sponsor and ask for an additional developer for the team
Ask the team to work extra hours for the next two sprints so that the velocity returns to its earlier level
questions.explanation: Hidden work is an impediment; making it visible lets the product owner and team plan capacity honestly. Overtime is not sustainable, asking for more people skips understanding the cause, and velocity is a planning measure, not a target to push.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a requirements traceability matrix?
options: To show which team member is responsible, accountable, consulted or informed for each deliverable
To link each requirement to its business objective and to the deliverables and tests that satisfy it
To rank each requirement by its probability of changing and by its impact on the project's schedule
To record the cost and duration estimates for each requirement in the project's scope baseline
questions.explanation: The traceability matrix links requirements to their origin and through to deliverables and tests, so nothing is lost and nothing unrequested is built. A RACI chart shows responsibilities, and probability and impact belong to risk analysis.

questions.stem: Your organization releases project funds quarterly. The cost baseline shows second-quarter spending above that quarter's funding limit. What should you do?
options: Cancel the work planned for the second quarter that exceeds the limit and remove it from the scope
Reschedule work to keep spending within the funding limit, and show the sponsor the schedule impact
Ask the team to delay invoices from suppliers until the third quarter so that the limit is not exceeded
Spend as planned in the second quarter and ask finance to cover the overspend from later quarters
questions.explanation: Funding limit reconciliation adjusts the timing of work so spending stays within available funds, which may move the schedule; the sponsor needs to understand that impact. Overspending, cutting scope without approval or delaying supplier invoices are not acceptable fixes.

questions.stem: Your team has developed a test approach that halved defect rates, and other projects in the company could benefit from it. What should you do?
options: Share it with the PMO so the organizational process assets can be updated
Keep it within the team, since it gives the project a competitive advantage
Send the approach directly to every project manager in the company by email
Wait until project closure and mention it in the final lessons learned report
questions.explanation: Continuous improvement includes updating organizational process assets so good practices reach other projects; the PMO usually owns them. Keeping it secret helps no one, waiting delays the benefit, and an uncoordinated email blast may not change standards.

questions.stem: On your hybrid project, the sponsor tells you that your monthly reports are accurate but do not help him. What should you do?
options: Ask the sponsor which decisions he needs to make and adjust the report to support them
Add more detail to the monthly reports so that the sponsor has every piece of information
Keep the reports as they are, because they are accurate and meet the governance standard
Ask the PMO for its standard report template and use it for the sponsor from next month
questions.explanation: A feedback loop means using the receiver's response to improve communication; reports should be aligned with what the sponsor needs to decide. More detail or a generic template may still miss the need, and accuracy alone does not make a report useful.

questions.stem: In a matrix organization, a functional manager tells you she is moving your database administrator to another project next week, in the middle of your current release. What should you do?
options: Meet with the functional manager to explain the impact and negotiate options
Tell the database administrator to keep working on your project regardless of her decision
Ask the sponsor to overrule the functional manager before speaking with her
Accept the decision and delay all database work until a new person is found
questions.explanation: In a matrix organization the project manager negotiates for resources with functional managers; explaining the impact and exploring options (timing, partial allocation, a replacement) comes first. Directing the employee against her manager, passively accepting or escalating first are poor choices.

questions.stem: A newly formed team is arguing about how the work should be done, and members are testing your authority and each other's. Which stage of team development is the team in?
options: Storming
Forming
Norming
Adjourning
questions.explanation: In the Tuckman model, storming is when members push back, compete and disagree about approach after the polite forming stage. Norming comes when they settle on how to work together, and adjourning is the team's close.

questions.stem: Which TWO are benefits of delivering value incrementally? (Choose two.)
options: Testing is no longer needed because each increment is small
Stakeholder engagement is not needed until the final release
Early feedback lowers the risk of building the wrong product
Users start to receive benefits before the whole project ends
The scope is guaranteed to stay fixed from the start to the end
questions.explanation: Incremental delivery gets feedback early and starts the flow of benefits sooner. Each increment still needs testing, scope is expected to evolve, and stakeholder engagement is needed throughout.

questions.stem: Your monthly report shows a cost variance that has gone beyond the threshold set in the cost management plan. What should you do?
options: Move money from the management reserve to the cost baseline to bring the variance back within limits
Ask the team to record their time under other projects until the variance is back within its limit
Keep reporting the variance in monthly reports and act only if it doubles over the next two months
Analyze the cause and follow the governance process set for variances beyond the threshold
questions.explanation: Thresholds exist to trigger analysis and the agreed governance response, such as escalation or a corrective action proposal. Using management reserve needs approval, waiting lets the problem grow, and misrecording time is unethical.

questions.stem: Your project's new system will change the daily tasks of 300 claims staff, and many are anxious about their jobs. What should you do?
options: Delay go-live until no staff member has any remaining concern about the change
Assess readiness and plan change management with HR and business leaders
Tell staff that their jobs are safe, without first checking with the business
Focus on delivering the system and leave the staff reaction to line managers
questions.explanation: Supporting organizational change means assessing the culture and readiness and planning communication, training and support with the business. Ignoring the people side risks adoption, waiting for zero concern is unrealistic, and unverified promises damage trust.

questions.stem: Which TWO practices help agile teams manage risk? (Choose two.)
options: Freezing scope at the start so that it never changes
A risk register that is reviewed only at phase gates
Spikes to explore uncertain technical questions
Short iterations that bring problems to light early
Making the product owner the owner of every risk
questions.explanation: Frequent delivery and feedback expose risks early, and spikes buy information to reduce technical uncertainty. Reviewing risks only at gates is too infrequent, freezing scope gives up adaptability, and one person owning every risk does not work.

questions.stem: Midway through your hybrid project, a contact at a government regulator asks to be kept informed because the project affects a licence the company holds. What should you do?
options: Send the contact the latest status report and add them to the existing distribution list
Tell the contact that the stakeholder list was finalized during planning and cannot be changed
Forward the request to the legal department, since dealing with regulators is outside the project
Add the contact to the stakeholder register, analyze their needs and update the engagement plan
questions.explanation: Stakeholder identification continues throughout the project. A new stakeholder is recorded, analyzed and planned for, which may call for a different communication approach than the standard report. Ignoring the regulator or handing it off without analysis creates risk.

questions.stem: The sponsor has started going directly to developers in the middle of a sprint to ask for small new features. The developers feel they cannot refuse. What should you do?
options: Explain to the sponsor how new requests reach the team through the product owner and the backlog
Ask the developers to log the hours spent on these requests so the cost can be reported later
Ask the product owner to cancel the sprint and start a new one that includes the sponsor's requests
Tell the developers to accept the sponsor's requests, since the sponsor is funding the project
questions.explanation: Part of leading an agile team is representing the team and protecting the sprint; requests go to the product owner, who prioritizes them in the backlog. Accepting side requests undermines the sprint goal, tracking hours does not fix the behavior, and cancelling a sprint is an extreme step reserved for an obsolete sprint goal.

questions.stem: The customer has formally accepted the final deliverable. Which TWO activities should you now complete? (Choose two.)
options: Close out procurements and confirm all contracts are settled
Finalize lessons learned and archive the project records
Begin collecting requirements for the next product release
Rebaseline the schedule to match the actual finish date
Hold sprint planning for the work after the final release
questions.explanation: Closure includes settling and closing contracts, finalizing lessons learned and archiving records. New requirements and sprint planning belong to future work, and rebaselining at closure would hide the performance record.

questions.stem: You are planning a project to build a new data center. The company has public targets for cutting energy use and emissions. When should sustainability requirements be addressed?
options: After go-live, once the data center's actual energy consumption has been measured
During planning, as requirements and acceptance criteria that shape the design
Only if the sponsor raises them, because they are not part of the project objectives
During closure, as part of the lessons learned for future data center projects
questions.explanation: Critical information requirements such as sustainability must be identified in planning so they shape design choices; retrofitting later is costly or impossible. Waiting for the sponsor ignores published company targets, and closure is too late to influence the result.

questions.stem: A kanban team wants to forecast delivery dates and improve the flow of work. Which TWO measures are most useful? (Choose two.)
options: Throughput
Earned value
Meetings held per week
Lines of code written
Cycle time
questions.explanation: Cycle time (how long an item takes from start to finish) and throughput (items finished per period) describe flow and support forecasting. Earned value suits a predictive baseline, and meeting counts and lines of code do not measure delivered value.

questions.stem: A new consumer protection regulation will take effect in four months, partway through your agile project. It affects how the app must display prices. What should you do?
options: Continue with the current backlog and deal with the regulation after release
Ask the team to add the changes quietly without updating the backlog or plan
Stop all development until the legal team publishes a full interpretation of it
Assess its impact on the backlog with the product owner and adjust priorities
questions.explanation: External changes are assessed for their impact on scope or backlog, and the product owner reprioritizes so the product is compliant by the deadline. Ignoring it, halting all work or making hidden changes are all poor responses.

questions.stem: The sales director expects the new portal to launch with full ordering features, while the support director expects a smaller launch with fewer support calls. Both are key stakeholders. What should you do?
options: Follow the sales director's expectations, since sales brings in the revenue that pays for the project
Ask the sponsor to decide between the two directors without first discussing it with either of them
Facilitate a discussion between them about expectations against the project objectives and agree priorities
Plan the scope to satisfy both directors fully, adding whatever time and budget to the baseline is needed
questions.explanation: Aligning expectations means facilitating a discussion that tests both against the project objectives and reaches agreed priorities. Picking a side or trying to satisfy everything avoids the conversation, and going to the sponsor before facilitating skips the project manager's role.

questions.stem: In design sessions, a senior engineer quickly dismisses ideas from junior team members, and the juniors have stopped contributing. What should you do?
options: Let the team sort it out, since self-organizing teams are expected to resolve their own dynamics
Have the junior members focus on building the designs and leave design decisions to the senior engineer
Ask the senior engineer to stop attending design sessions so that junior members feel free to speak
Use a facilitation technique such as silent brainstorming so every idea is captured before discussion
questions.explanation: Structured facilitation gives every voice a fair hearing and makes use of the team's varied perspectives. Removing the senior engineer loses expertise, leaving it alone lets the pattern continue, and sidelining juniors wastes their ideas.

questions.stem: You find that your team shares a single administrator password for the production database. What should you do?
options: Ask the team to stop using the database until the end of the project to remove the risk
Change the password yourself and send the new one to every team member in a group message
Record it in the risk register and agree a mitigation with IT security, such as individual accounts
Leave the setup as it is, since no security incident has happened on the project so far
questions.explanation: Poor IT security practice is a project risk; it is recorded, owned and mitigated with the security experts, for example through individual, auditable accounts. Sharing a new password repeats the problem, past luck is no control, and stopping all database use is not workable.

questions.stem: Several defects that an automated regression test would have caught reached users in the last two releases. What should the agile team do?
options: Add automated regression tests to its definition of done
Add a separate testing phase after each sprint is complete
Ask users to test each release before it goes to everyone
Slow the release cadence from every sprint to every quarter
questions.explanation: Building quality in means updating the definition of done so every item is covered by automated regression tests before it counts as finished. A separate test phase or slower releases delay feedback, and making users test shifts the team's quality work onto customers.

questions.stem: While integrating the subsidiary plans, you see that the resource plan has the lead tester on another project during the test phase in the schedule. What should you do?
options: Baseline the plan as it is and raise a change request once the test phase is about to begin
Ask the lead tester to work on both projects at the same time during the test phase
Resolve the conflict between the plans before the project management plan is baselined
Remove the test phase from the schedule, since no lead tester will be available for it
questions.explanation: Integrating the plan means finding and fixing gaps and conflicts between the subsidiary plans before baselining. Baselining a known conflict, dropping testing or overloading the tester all create predictable problems.

questions.stem: Team members keep project documents in their personal drives, and stakeholders often work from old versions. What should you do?
options: Set up a shared, version-controlled repository that the right stakeholders can access
Ask each team member to keep a list of their documents and send it to you each week
Email the latest version of every document to all stakeholders whenever it changes
Print the key documents and keep them in a binder in the project office for reference
questions.explanation: Artifacts must be accessible, current and controlled. A shared repository with version control gives one source of truth. Emailing every change floods inboxes and still creates copies, personal lists do not solve access, and printed binders go out of date.

questions.stem: During a bid evaluation, one of the competing vendors offers you expensive tickets to a sports final. What should you do?
options: Decline the tickets and follow the organization's policy on gifts
Ask the vendor to give the tickets to a team member who is not involved
Accept the tickets, since they will not affect your bid evaluation
Accept the tickets and disclose them after the contract is awarded
questions.explanation: Accepting gifts from a bidder creates a conflict of interest or its appearance, against both ethics codes and procurement policy. Disclosing later or redirecting the gift does not remove the conflict.

questions.stem: A key stakeholder complains that she was never told about an approved change that affects her department. What should you do first?
options: Apologize and send her the change log so she can review all approved changes herself
Add her to every project distribution list so that she never misses information again
Review the communication management plan to see how her information needs were captured
Ask the change control board to explain to her why the change was approved without her input
questions.explanation: The first step is to find the cause: whether her needs were missed in the communication plan or the plan was not followed. Sending a log or adding her to every list treats the symptom, and the change board did not cause the communication gap.

questions.stem: Some team members have started using a generative AI tool to draft test cases. Others worry about accuracy and about company data being entered into the tool. What is the best action?
options: Let each team member decide individually whether and how to use the tool for their own work
Allow unrestricted use of the tool, since it shortens test preparation and the team can always fix any errors it finds later
Facilitate the team in agreeing ground rules for AI use, including human review and data handling, within company policy
Ban the tool on the project until the organization has finished evaluating generative AI products
questions.explanation: Agreeing team norms for AI, such as review of outputs and what data may be shared, within organizational policy, captures the benefit while addressing both concerns. A blanket ban gives up the benefit, unrestricted use ignores real risks, and individual choices leave the team without shared rules.

questions.stem: Read the case study. The installation contractor's field lead and the app team lead disagree about the data format the new meters will send. Each says the other side must change. What should you do?
options: Raise the disagreement with the steering committee and ask it to choose one of the two formats
Tell the contractor to adapt to the app team's format, because the app delivers the business case
Tell the app team to adapt to the contractor's format, because the fixed-price contract is already signed
Bring both leads together to review what each side needs and agree an interface both can support
questions.explanation: This is a conflict over a shared interface, so the project manager first brings the parties together to solve the problem collaboratively. Imposing either side's format is forcing without analysis, and the steering committee is an escalation path for when the project cannot resolve it.

questions.stem: Read the case study. Steering committee members say the monthly report is too long, and the city council will soon need its first quarterly update. How should you plan reporting for these two groups?
options: Decision-focused monthly reports for the committee and a plain quarterly summary of progress and benefits for the council
One detailed report that goes to both groups, so that the council and the committee always see the same information
Monthly reports only for the steering committee, with the general manager briefing the council from them as needed
A full technical report for the council each quarter, since councillors may face detailed questions from residents about it
questions.explanation: Reporting should be aligned with each audience: the committee governs the project and needs decision-focused reports, while the council needs a concise view of progress and the public benefits, such as water loss. One report for all misses both needs, and leaving the council to secondhand briefings ignores a key stakeholder.

questions.stem: Read the case study. What is the schedule performance index (SPI) of the installation track at the end of phase 2? Round to two decimal places. Type the number only.
questions.explanation: SPI = EV / PV = 800,000 / 1,000,000 = 0.80. Only 80 percent of the planned installation work is done. CPI = EV / AC = 1.00, so the work done has cost exactly what was planned.

questions.stem: Read the case study. The installation contractor is behind schedule and asks for extra payment to add crews and catch up. What should you do?
options: Accept the delay and move the start of phase 3 later without discussing it with the contractor
Pay the extra amount from the contingency reserve so that phase 3 can still start on its originally planned date
Terminate the contract for default and find a new contractor to install the remaining meters
Review the contract with procurement and ask the contractor for a recovery plan within the agreed price
questions.explanation: Under a fixed-price contract the seller generally bears the cost of meeting its obligations, so the first step is to check the contract terms and ask for a recovery plan at the agreed price. Paying extra without a contract change, terminating at the first problem or silently accepting the delay all mismanage the contract.

questions.stem: Read the case study. How should you respond to the privacy regulator's draft guidance on storing hourly usage data?
options: Leave the matter to the meter contractor, since the meters are what collect and send the hourly usage data
Stop collecting hourly data immediately and remove the leak alerts from the app until the guidance is final
Wait until the guidance is final before discussing it, since draft guidance has no legal force on the utility
With the privacy officer, assess how the guidance affects the app backlog and data design, and plan for it
questions.explanation: Changes in the external environment are monitored and assessed early for their impact on scope and backlog. Working with the privacy officer lets the team design for likely rules without overreacting. Waiting removes time to adapt, dropping leak alerts undermines the business case, and the utility, not the contractor, is accountable for data handling.

questions.stem: During a sprint review, a developer and a quality assurance analyst begin openly criticizing each other's work in front of stakeholders. What should you do first?
options: Continue the meeting and let them finish the argument, since the stakeholders may want to hear both sides
Pause the discussion and meet with both of them privately afterward to understand the disagreement
Report the incident to the quality manager and ask for the analyst to be replaced on the project
Tell the two of them in the meeting that the quality analyst's view is final on quality matters
questions.explanation: A conflict is best handled in private and by first understanding its source. Ruling in public is forcing, letting an argument play out before stakeholders harms the team, and replacing someone before understanding the issue is premature.

questions.stem: A group of field technicians has just been identified as stakeholders. What should you do before choosing how to communicate with them?
options: Add them to the existing weekly status email distribution
Ask the sponsor which communication method to use with them
Wait until they ask for information so that effort is not wasted
Analyze their interests, influence and information needs
questions.explanation: Stakeholder analysis comes before planning engagement and communication, so the method fits their needs. Defaulting to the existing email, deferring to the sponsor or waiting for requests all skip that analysis.

questions.stem: You are leading development of a medical device with embedded software. Regulators require full design documentation and formal verification, and the user interface needs to be refined with clinicians. Which approach fits best?
options: Purely predictive: all user interface details are frozen before design starts, and clinicians see only the finished device
Hybrid: predictive control of the regulated documents and verification, with iterative work on the interface
Purely adaptive: the team releases every two weeks and writes the regulatory documentation at the end
Kanban only: work items flow continuously and the regulatory documentation is left out of the project scope
questions.explanation: A hybrid approach combines the formal control regulators require with iteration where learning from users matters. Leaving documentation to the end or out of scope breaks compliance, and freezing the interface without clinician feedback risks a poor product.

questions.stem: A project has an earned value of \$45,000 and a planned value of \$50,000. What is the schedule variance? Type the number only, with no commas or currency sign, and use a minus sign if it is negative.
questions.explanation: SV = EV - PV = 45,000 - 50,000 = -5,000. A negative schedule variance means less work has been done than planned.

questions.stem: You learn that a developer changed an interface specification without approval. The change made integration faster, and the customer is pleased. What should you do?
options: Leave the change as it is, since the customer is pleased and integration went faster as a result
Reverse the change at once, whatever it costs, because it never went through the change control process
Assess and document the change, take it through change control, and remind the team of the process
Report the developer to human resources for a breach of the project's change control procedures
questions.explanation: Unapproved changes still need to be evaluated and recorded through change control, because they may affect other work, documentation or contracts; the team also needs a reminder of the process. Ignoring it, reversing it without analysis or punishing the developer are not appropriate first responses.

questions.stem: Your team is deciding whether to develop a training module in-house or buy one from a vendor. Which technique should it use?
options: Monte Carlo analysis
Root cause analysis
Earned value analysis
Make-or-buy analysis
questions.explanation: Make-or-buy analysis compares the cost, risk, capability and timing of doing the work internally against buying it. Earned value measures performance, root cause analysis finds causes of problems and Monte Carlo analysis models uncertainty.

questions.stem: Your team has raised four impediments at once. Which should you work on first?
options: The one that will be quickest for you to resolve on your own
The one raised by the most senior developer on the team
The one that was raised first by the team, a few days ago
The one blocking the most valuable work in the current sprint
questions.explanation: Impediments are prioritized by their impact on delivering value, so the one blocking the most important sprint work comes first. Ease, order of arrival or the seniority of the person raising it do not reflect impact.

questions.stem: Integration testing keeps failing, and the hardware team and the software team blame each other in every meeting. What is the best approach?
options: Hold separate meetings for each team so that they no longer meet until the integration phase is finished
Bring both teams together to analyze the failures and agree on a shared way of working at the interface
Assign one team the responsibility for all integration defects so accountability is clear from now on
Ask each team to document its own view of the failures and send the documents to the sponsor
questions.explanation: The conflict comes from a shared interface, so a joint analysis focused on the problem rather than on people resolves it. Assigning blame, escalating competing documents or keeping the teams apart all leave the cause in place.

questions.stem: A client manager who is new to agile attends sprint reviews but says very little and later sends long lists of complaints by email. What should you do?
options: Coach the client manager on the purpose of sprint reviews and the kind of feedback that helps most
Ask the product owner to stop inviting the client manager to sprint reviews and to send summaries instead
Ask the team to answer each emailed complaint in writing before starting work on the next sprint
Escalate the emails to the client's sponsor as evidence that the client manager is not engaged
questions.explanation: Mentoring and coaching stakeholders on how to take part is part of aligning expectations; once the client manager knows how reviews work, feedback can be given and discussed in the review. Excluding the person, answering by email or escalating does not build engagement.

questions.stem: Which of these does a project scope statement include?
options: The resource calendars and named team assignments
The risk register with its owners and responses
The detailed activity durations and their dependencies
The deliverables, acceptance criteria and exclusions
questions.explanation: The scope statement describes the product scope, deliverables, acceptance criteria, assumptions, constraints and exclusions. Resource calendars, activity durations and the risk register are separate project documents.

questions.stem: A project has a budget at completion of \$100,000, an earned value of \$40,000 and an actual cost of \$50,000. What to-complete performance index (TCPI) is needed to finish within the original budget? Round to one decimal place. Type the number only.
questions.explanation: TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = (100,000 - 40,000) / (100,000 - 50,000) = 60,000 / 50,000 = 1.2. The remaining work must be done at a cost efficiency of 1.2, much better than the current CPI of 0.8, which is unlikely without corrective action.

questions.stem: In the middle of a sprint, a stakeholder asks to change a story the team is already working on. The change is not urgent. What should happen?
options: The project manager submits the change to the change control board
The team changes the story at once to keep the stakeholder satisfied
The team stops the sprint and replans with the stakeholder's change
The product owner adds the change to the backlog for a future sprint
questions.explanation: Non-urgent changes during a sprint go to the product owner, who orders them in the backlog so the sprint goal stays stable. Changing scope mid-sprint, using a predictive change board for a backlog item, or stopping the sprint are not warranted.

questions.stem: You are about to issue a request for proposal. What should be defined before the proposals arrive?
options: The lessons learned from closing out the procurement
The name of the seller that is expected to win the work
The final contract price that the buyer is willing to pay
The source selection criteria for evaluating proposals
