questions.explanation: Source selection criteria are set before proposals are received so every seller is evaluated fairly against the same standards. Fixing a price or a winner in advance undermines the competition, and closeout lessons come at the end.

questions.stem: Your project is blocked by a dispute between two departments over who owns some customer data. Resolving it is outside your authority. What should you do?
options: Decide which department owns the data, since the project needs an answer
Wait for the two departments to resolve the dispute between themselves
Work around the dispute by copying the data into a new project database
Escalate it to the sponsor with its impact on the project and the options
questions.explanation: Issues beyond the project manager's authority are escalated through governance, with the impact and options so the decision can be made quickly. Deciding for the departments oversteps authority, waiting leaves the project blocked, and copying disputed data may create a compliance problem.

questions.stem: Your new team is made up mostly of junior staff who have not used the project's tools before. Which leadership approach is most appropriate at the start?
options: Delegate all decisions to the team from day one so that members learn by solving problems
Keep a hands-off role and step in only when a deadline is about to be missed
Focus on rewards and penalties tied to each person's weekly output to keep productivity high
Give clear direction and hands-on coaching, then delegate more as the team builds skill
questions.explanation: Situational leadership matches style to the team's readiness: more direction and coaching for an inexperienced team, more delegation as competence grows. Full delegation or a hands-off approach sets a junior team up to struggle, and pure reward-and-penalty management does not build skill.

questions.stem: At the last steering meeting, a key stakeholder was surprised by a schedule delay that you announced, and she has been cool toward the project since. What should you do differently?
options: Brief her early and privately about significant bad news before it reaches formal meetings
Ask the sponsor to deliver all bad news to her in future, since the sponsor has more authority
Leave bad news out of the steering meetings and report it in the written monthly report only
Present only recovery plans in future meetings and leave the delays themselves out of them
questions.explanation: Trust is built by transparency and no surprises; key stakeholders should hear significant news early and in the right setting. Hiding or softening bad news damages trust further, and handing the message to the sponsor avoids the project manager's responsibility.

questions.stem: Stakeholders cannot explain what they want from a new customer portal, but they say they will know it when they see it. Which technique is most useful for gathering requirements?
options: Ask the team to write the requirements based on their experience
Send them a detailed questionnaire to complete individually
Build a simple prototype and gather their feedback on it
Wait until the stakeholders can describe their needs in writing
questions.explanation: Prototypes give stakeholders something concrete to react to, which surfaces needs they cannot describe in the abstract. Questionnaires assume they can articulate needs, team-written requirements may miss the real ones, and waiting delays the project.

questions.passage:
| Activity | Duration (days) | Predecessor |
|---|---|---|
| A | 3 | none |
| B | 4 | A |
| C | 7 | A |
| D | 2 | B |
| E | 3 | C and D |
questions.stem: Use the network below. What is the duration of the critical path in days? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: Path A-B-D-E = 3 + 4 + 2 + 3 = 12 days. Path A-C-E = 3 + 7 + 3 = 13 days. The longest path, A-C-E, is the critical path, so the project takes 13 days.

questions.stem: What is the main role of a project steering committee?
options: To test the deliverables before they are handed over to the customer
To manage the team's daily work and assign tasks to individual members
To write the detailed requirements for each deliverable in the project
To give direction, approve major changes and resolve escalated issues
questions.explanation: A steering committee is a governance body that provides direction, makes decisions above the project manager's authority and resolves escalations. Daily task management, requirements writing and testing are delivery work.

questions.stem: A newly formed agile team is about to start its first sprint. Which should the team establish first?
options: Individual velocity targets for each team member
A detailed task schedule covering the next six sprints
A list of team members ranked by seniority
Working agreements and a shared definition of done
questions.explanation: Working agreements and a definition of done set the expectations a team needs to work together and judge when work is finished. Velocity is a team measure, not an individual target, detailed six-sprint task schedules contradict iterative planning, and seniority rankings do not help a self-organizing team.

questions.stem: How should an agile team best keep track of whether its customer remains satisfied as the product evolves?
options: Ask the team members to rate how happy they believe the customer is
Assume satisfaction for as long as the customer raises no formal complaints
Gather feedback at each sprint review and track satisfaction over time
Run one detailed satisfaction survey when the final release is done
questions.explanation: Frequent feedback at reviews, tracked over time, lets the team respond while it can still change course. A single final survey is too late, silence does not mean satisfaction, and the team's guess is not the customer's view.

questions.stem: A colleague reviewing your WBS asks why project management work appears in it. Which principle explains this?
options: The WBS includes all of the work in the project and nothing outside its scope
The WBS only shows the product deliverables that the customer will accept
The WBS lists the work in the order it will be done, starting with management
The WBS includes the work that the project team finds hardest to estimate
questions.explanation: The 100 percent rule: the WBS captures all of the work, including project management, and excludes anything outside scope. It is not limited to product deliverables and is not a sequence of work.

questions.stem: What does the estimate to complete (ETC) represent?
options: The expected cost to finish all remaining project work
The total expected cost of the project when it is done
The difference between the budget and the final cost
The value of the work completed so far on the project
questions.explanation: ETC is the expected cost of the remaining work (EAC - AC). EAC is the total expected cost, VAC is the budget minus EAC, and EV is the value of work completed.

questions.stem: Stakeholders are confused about which change requests have been approved, rejected or are still pending. What should you do?
options: Keep a change log that stakeholders can see and report on its status
Hold a meeting to repeat every change decision made since the kickoff
Ask the change control board to email each requester its decision
Stop accepting new change requests until the confusion is resolved
questions.explanation: Communicating the status of proposed changes is part of change control; a visible change log with regular reporting gives everyone one current source. Individual emails do not reach other affected stakeholders, a one-off meeting soon goes out of date, and refusing requests is not a fix.

questions.stem: You are preparing to negotiate a support contract with a vendor. What should you do before the negotiation begins?
options: Agree to the vendor's standard terms so the meeting goes smoothly
Decide your priorities, acceptable trade-offs and walk-away position
Ask the vendor to share its internal costs so you can set the price
Invite the whole project team so that everyone can speak for the buyer
questions.explanation: A negotiation strategy sets priorities, trade-offs and a walk-away point in advance. Accepting standard terms gives up the negotiation, vendors rarely share internal costs, and a crowded room with many voices weakens the buyer's position.

questions.stem: Your risk register has 60 identified risks. Which tool helps you quickly prioritize them for further attention?
options: A requirements traceability matrix
A responsibility assignment matrix
A probability and impact matrix
A stakeholder engagement matrix
questions.explanation: Qualitative risk analysis uses a probability and impact matrix to rate and rank risks so attention goes to the highest priorities. The other matrices cover roles, requirements and stakeholders.

questions.stem: One of the strongest developers on your agile team has become quiet and disengaged. In conversation, they mention they feel they are not learning anything new. What should you do?
options: Mention the disengagement to the functional manager so it is noted before the annual review
Explore the member's development goals and look for project work that builds the skills they want
Ask the functional manager to approve a one-time bonus to recognize the member's past performance
Take no action for now, because the member's deliverables are still on time and of good quality
questions.explanation: Motivation that comes from growth is addressed by connecting the person to meaningful development, which a project manager can often do through assignments. A bonus does not answer the stated need, ignoring it risks losing the person, and reporting it as a problem damages trust.

questions.stem: Select the communication method each example uses.
rows: A weekly status email sent to a distribution list
A project wiki that stakeholders read when they choose
A video call to resolve a disputed requirement
Recorded training videos on the intranet
A workshop to agree on acceptance criteria
questions.explanation: Push communication is sent to recipients (emails, memos). Pull communication is placed where people access it when they choose (wikis, intranet libraries). Interactive communication is a real-time exchange (calls, meetings, workshops) and is best for resolving disagreements and reaching agreement.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a user story's acceptance criteria and the team's definition of done?
options: Acceptance criteria are specific to one story, while the definition of done applies to every story
Acceptance criteria are written by the team, while the definition of done is written by the customer
There is no difference, because the two terms describe the same checklist used in sprint reviews
Acceptance criteria apply only to the final release, while the definition of done applies to each sprint
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria describe what one story must do to be accepted; the definition of done is the shared quality checklist (tested, reviewed, documented) that every item must meet. They are different and both apply in every sprint.

questions.stem: Concrete must cure for 3 days after it is poured before the framing can start. How should this be shown in the schedule?
options: As 3 days of float on the framing activity in the schedule
As a 3-day lead on the dependency between pouring and framing
As a start-to-start dependency between pouring and framing
As a 3-day lag on the dependency between pouring and framing
questions.explanation: A lag is a required wait between activities: framing starts 3 days after pouring finishes. A lead would let framing start before pouring finishes, float is flexibility rather than a requirement, and start-to-start would let both begin together.

questions.stem: How should you measure the extent to which your project complies with its regulatory requirements?
options: Ask the team members whether they feel the project is compliant
Count the number of compliance documents the project has produced
Audit deliverables and processes against each requirement
Assume compliance unless the regulator raises a formal concern
questions.explanation: Measuring compliance means checking evidence (deliverables, records, processes) against each requirement, often through audits or checklists. Opinions, the absence of complaints or document counts do not show compliance.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a quality audit on a project?
options: To confirm the project follows its quality processes and find improvements
To measure the team's productivity so that low performers can be identified
To inspect each deliverable and reject the ones with defects before delivery
To approve the final deliverables on behalf of the customer at project closure
questions.explanation: A quality audit is an independent review of whether the project is following its quality policies and processes, and it identifies good practices and gaps. Inspecting deliverables is quality control, and acceptance is done by the customer.

questions.stem: To avoid a risk of supplier delay, your team decides to make a component in-house. This creates a new risk that the team lacks the needed skills. What is this new risk called?
options: A residual risk
A trigger condition
A secondary risk
A workaround
questions.explanation: A secondary risk arises directly from carrying out a risk response. A residual risk is what remains after a response, a trigger is a sign that a risk is about to occur, and a workaround is an unplanned response to an issue.

questions.stem: On a hybrid project, the product owner and the sponsor describe the minimum viable product differently, and the team is getting conflicting direction. What should you do?
options: Ask the team to build the features from both versions so the conflict can be settled at the demo
Facilitate a session with the sponsor and product owner to agree the product vision and the scope of the MVP
Follow the product owner's version, because the product owner is the person accountable for the product backlog
Follow the sponsor's version, because the sponsor is accountable for the project's funding and benefits
questions.explanation: The root cause is a vision that is not shared by two key stakeholders; the project manager facilitates alignment between them. Picking either person's version leaves the other misaligned and the conflict will return, and building both wastes capacity.

questions.stem: Your stakeholders are spread across five time zones, and many complain that the weekly live status meeting is at an unreasonable hour for them. What should you do?
options: Publish a short recorded update with written highlights, and keep live sessions only for decisions
Keep the meeting time as it is, since any time chosen will be inconvenient for somebody on the team
Move the meeting each week to a new time slot and require every stakeholder to attend each session
Cancel the status meeting and ask stakeholders to contact the team members directly when needed
questions.explanation: Asynchronous updates suit routine status across time zones, and live time is saved for decisions that need interaction. Ignoring the complaint, adding mandatory rotating meetings or sending people to the team directly all make communication worse.

questions.stem: Two backlog features have the same business value. Feature A takes two weeks of work, and Feature B takes six weeks. Delaying either costs the business the same amount per week. Which should be done first?
options: Feature B, because larger features are more important to the customer
Feature B, because it carries more risk and should be started first
Feature A, because it delivers the same value sooner for less effort
Either one, because value per week of delay is the same for both
questions.explanation: With equal value and equal cost of delay, the shorter job delivers value sooner and reduces the total delay cost; this is the idea behind weighted shortest job first. Size does not mean importance, and nothing in the case suggests Feature B is riskier.

questions.stem: Select the type of each dependency.
rows: The walls cannot be painted before they are built
The team prefers to write the user guide once the screens are stable
Installation cannot start until the city issues a permit
The contract requires an audit before the final payment is released
questions.explanation: Mandatory (hard logic) dependencies come from the nature of the work or from contracts and law. Discretionary (preferred logic) dependencies reflect a team choice and can be changed to compress the schedule. External dependencies rely on parties outside the project, such as a permitting authority.

questions.stem: You discover that a software vendor stores your project's customer data in a country where your company's data residency rules do not allow it. What should you do?
options: Ignore the issue, since the vendor is responsible for where it chooses to store data
Ask the vendor to keep the data where it is until the contract ends, and only then to move it elsewhere
End the contract at once and move the data yourself without involving the vendor
Assess the noncompliance with your compliance team and agree corrective action with the vendor
questions.explanation: Noncompliance is analyzed with the right experts for its consequences, then corrective action is agreed with the vendor under the contract. Postponing or ignoring it leaves the company in breach, and unilateral action may breach the contract and cause data loss.

questions.stem: At a retrospective, several team members say the working agreements they wrote at the start are no longer being followed and some no longer make sense. What should happen next?
options: The product owner decides which of the agreements stay in force
You rewrite the working agreements and present the new version
The team reviews its working agreements together and updates them
The team drops the agreements and relies on everyday common sense
questions.explanation: Working agreements belong to the team and should evolve; a retrospective is the right place for the team to revise them. Agreements written by the project manager or product owner lose ownership, and dropping them removes the shared norms.

questions.stem: Your team has found a defect that will push the release date back by two weeks. The sponsor is preparing to announce the release date to customers tomorrow. What should you do?
options: Mention the defect in the next monthly report as a schedule risk to be monitored
Tell the sponsor today about the defect, its impact and the recovery options
Ask the team to work through the weekend before deciding whether to tell anyone
Let the announcement go ahead and look for ways to recover the two weeks later
questions.explanation: Transparency requires sharing bad news promptly, especially before the sponsor commits the organization publicly. Letting the announcement go ahead, hoping overtime fixes it, or downgrading a known delay to a risk in a later report all breach that duty.

questions.stem: Six months into a two-year project, a competitor launches a product that cuts the expected market share of your project's product by half. What should you do?
options: Reduce the project's scope to cut costs without first discussing the change with the sponsor
Review the business case with the sponsor to confirm the project still delivers enough value
Ask the team to speed up the work so the product reaches the market before more competition
Continue as planned, since the business case was approved before the project started work
questions.explanation: Business value must be examined throughout the project. A major market change means the sponsor needs to decide, with updated analysis, whether to continue, change direction or stop. Continuing blindly, rushing or cutting scope alone skips that decision.

questions.stem: Two critical activities need the same specialist at the same time, and no one else has the skill. You apply resource leveling. What is the likely result?
options: The critical path will be removed entirely
The project finish date will move earlier
The project finish date may move later
The project budget will drop significantly
questions.explanation: Resource leveling adjusts start and finish dates to fit limited resources; when the over-allocated resource is on the critical path, the project usually takes longer. It does not shorten the schedule or remove the critical path.

questions.stem: A business analyst is assigned 100 percent to your project and 50 percent to another project during the same month. What should you do?
options: Remove the analyst's tasks from your project and leave the requirements work until next quarter
Work with the other project manager and the functional manager to agree the analyst's priorities
Tell the other project manager that your project's allocation was approved first and takes priority
Ask the analyst to work extra hours so that both projects get the time they were promised
questions.explanation: Over-allocation across projects is resolved by the people who control the work and the resource agreeing priorities, sometimes with portfolio input. Overtime is not a sustainable fix, claiming priority damages relationships, and dropping the work creates a gap.

questions.stem: Your team's retrospective produced a list of nine improvement ideas. What is the best next step?
options: Pick one or two to act on, and add them to the next sprint's work
Implement all nine at once so the team improves as fast as it can
Record all nine ideas in the lessons register for future projects
Send all nine ideas to the PMO and wait for it to approve them
questions.explanation: Retrospectives work best when the team commits to a small number of improvements and makes them visible work. Trying all nine overwhelms the team, waiting for approval slows learning, and recording them without action changes nothing.

questions.stem: Select the opportunity response strategy shown by each action.
rows: Assign your best engineers so an early-finish bonus is certain
Partner with another firm to win a contract neither could win alone
Add resources to raise the chance of finishing early
Take the benefit if it happens, without pursuing it
questions.explanation: Exploiting tries to make sure the opportunity happens, enhancing raises its probability or impact, sharing gives part of it to a partner better able to capture it, and accepting takes it if it comes.

questions.stem: You are leading a newly formed team whose members have never met in person. Which TWO actions will most help build trust? (Choose two.)
options: Communicate only by email so there is always a written record of decisions
Agree communication norms such as expected response times and core hours
Monitor each person's online status to confirm they are working their hours
Hold a video kickoff where members share their backgrounds and working styles
Divide the work so that members rarely need to depend on one another
questions.explanation: Getting to know each other and agreeing how to communicate are foundations of trust in a virtual team. Monitoring online status signals distrust, email-only communication is slow and impersonal, and avoiding interdependence prevents trust from ever being built.

questions.stem: Which TWO are main purposes of a project kickoff meeting? (Choose two.)
options: Align stakeholders on the objectives, scope and success criteria
Introduce the roles, responsibilities and ways of communicating
Approve the change requests submitted so far in the project
Baseline the detailed schedule for every work package
Close the procurement agreements with the chosen suppliers
questions.explanation: A kickoff builds a shared understanding of objectives and success and sets out who does what and how the project will communicate. Baselining, approving changes and closing procurements are separate project activities with their own processes.

questions.stem: Your newly formed agile team has no historical velocity data, and the sponsor wants to know roughly how many sprints the first release will take. What is the best approach?
options: Have the team estimate the backlog with relative sizing, give a range, and refine it as velocity data comes in
Use the velocity of a different, experienced team in the company to calculate an exact date for the first release
Refuse to estimate until the team has finished five sprints and has a reliable average velocity
Ask the product owner to estimate the whole backlog alone so that the team is not distracted from work
questions.explanation: The people doing the work estimate it, relative sizing (for example planning poker) works without history, and a range honestly reflects uncertainty that shrinks as real velocity data arrives. Another team's velocity does not transfer, and refusing to estimate does not help the sponsor plan.

questions.stem: On a release burnup chart, the completed work line is rising at a steady rate, but the total scope line has risen faster for the last four sprints. What does this indicate?
options: Scope is growing faster than the team completes work, so the release date is at risk
The team's velocity is falling, so the team needs coaching on how to estimate stories
The team has stopped working on the release and is spending its time on support tickets
The release is on track, because the completed work line is still rising at a steady rate
questions.explanation: A burnup chart shows completed work and total scope separately. A steady completion rate with faster scope growth means the gap is widening; the product owner and stakeholders need to decide on scope or date. Velocity is steady, and the team is clearly still delivering.

questions.stem: A team is using the plan-do-check-act cycle to improve its handoff process. Select the stage for each step.
rows: Identify the problem and propose a change
Try the change on a small scale
Study the results against what was expected
Adopt the change as standard practice
questions.explanation: Plan defines the problem and the change, Do trials it on a small scale, Check compares results with expectations, and Act standardizes the change (or starts a new cycle).

questions.stem: A normally calm team member has become short-tempered with colleagues since the company announced a reorganization. What should you do first?
options: Remind the whole team about the code of conduct at the next team meeting
Check in privately with the team member and listen to their concerns
Ask human resources to speak with the member about the behavior
Reassign the member's tasks until the reorganization is complete
questions.explanation: Emotional intelligence starts with noticing a change and listening. A team-wide reminder does not reach the cause, involving human resources first escalates too quickly, and removing work may add to the person's worry.

questions.stem: Without talking to the team, the product owner promised a key customer that a large new feature would be ready in the next release. The team believes it cannot be done in time. What should you do?
options: Remove the feature from the backlog until the customer agrees to wait for a release after the next one
Ask the team to commit to the feature anyway so that the product owner's promise to the customer is kept
Tell the customer directly that the product owner made a mistake and that the feature will not be ready
Help the product owner and team size the feature, then present the customer with realistic options
questions.explanation: The expectation was set without the people who do the work; the right move is to estimate the work with the team and then reset the customer's expectations with real options, supporting the product owner rather than undermining them. Forcing a commitment risks quality and burnout.

questions.stem: Two developers on your team will be on leave for half of the next sprint. How should the team plan the sprint?
options: Postpone the sprint until both of the developers are back
Plan the usual amount of work and ask others to cover the gap
Plan the sprint using its capacity, adjusted for the time off
Extend the sprint by a week so the usual amount of work fits
questions.explanation: Sprint planning uses the team's real capacity, so a team with less availability commits to less work. Overcommitting, changing the sprint length or pausing the cadence all undermine predictability.

questions.stem: Your construction project's outdoor work is planned for midsummer, and the region has had more frequent extreme heat events in recent years. What should you do?
options: Add a large buffer to every activity in the schedule, outdoor or not, to cover any possible delays
Ignore it, because weather is outside the project's control and cannot be managed by the project team
Analyze the risk and plan a response, such as rescheduling some outdoor work and monitoring forecasts
Wait until the first heat event happens and then decide how the work should be rescheduled
questions.explanation: Climate and sustainability-related risks are analyzed and planned for like any other: the cause is uncontrollable, but the response is not. Waiting turns a risk into an issue, and blanket buffers on all activities hide the real exposure.

questions.stem: Which technique plans near-term work in detail and later work at a higher level, adding detail as more becomes known?
options: Critical chain method
Rolling wave planning
Fast tracking
Resource leveling
questions.explanation: Rolling wave planning is progressive elaboration of the plan over time. Critical chain manages buffers and resources, resource leveling resolves over-allocation, and fast tracking overlaps activities to compress the schedule.

questions.stem: How is the total project budget related to the cost baseline?
options: The project budget is the cost baseline plus the management reserve
The project budget is the cost baseline minus the contingency reserve
The project budget is the cost baseline plus the actual cost to date
The project budget and the cost baseline are always exactly the same
questions.explanation: The cost baseline (work package estimates plus contingency reserves) is what performance is measured against; adding the management reserve gives the total project budget.

questions.stem: Your company is moving to agile delivery, but its culture is strongly hierarchical. Teams keep waiting for managers to approve routine decisions, and progress is slow. What should you do?
options: Ask the managers to approve decisions faster so that the teams wait for a shorter time
Assess the culture and coach managers to delegate routine decisions to teams step by step
Return to predictive delivery, since agile methods do not work in a hierarchical company
Tell the teams to stop asking for approval and make every decision themselves from now on
questions.explanation: Organizational change needs an assessment of the culture and a deliberate plan, such as coaching managers to delegate gradually. Ordering teams to ignore managers creates conflict, giving up on agile ignores the strategy, and faster approvals keep the bottleneck.

questions.stem: Your team has spent two meetings debating which test automation tool to adopt and needs a decision by the end of the week. What is the best way to move forward?
options: Use a quick group decision technique such as fist of five, then discuss the objections it reveals
Ask the sponsor to pick the tool, since it will be paid for from the project budget
Choose the tool yourself, since the team has already spent too long on the decision
Postpone the choice until a later sprint, when the team will have more time to evaluate every candidate tool
questions.explanation: Fist of five and similar techniques show the level of support quickly and surface the specific concerns to resolve, keeping the decision with the team. Deciding for the team or handing it to the sponsor removes ownership, and postponing ignores the deadline.

questions.stem: Your PMO requires a monthly earned value report, but the agile team tracks progress with release burnup charts. What is the best approach?
options: Produce the earned value report yourself each month without telling the team how the figures are built
Agree with the PMO how the agile measures map to its reporting needs and report on that basis
Ignore the PMO requirement, because earned value reporting does not apply to agile teams
Ask the team to stop using burnup charts and track their work in earned value terms instead
questions.explanation: Hybrid reporting works by agreeing with governance bodies how adaptive measures (for example completed story points against the release plan) satisfy their needs. Forcing one method on the other, ignoring governance or reporting behind the team's back all cause problems.

questions.stem: Your project will hand a new billing system to the operations team next week. Operations staff say they have not been trained and do not know how to handle the overnight batch jobs. What should you do?
options: Ask the project team to run the batch jobs indefinitely after the system goes live
Confirm the transition criteria with operations and arrange the training before handover
Report to the sponsor that operations is not ready and close the project on schedule
Hand over on schedule, since operations can learn the batch jobs as and when problems arise
questions.explanation: Validating readiness for transition is part of closure; agreed criteria (training, documentation, support) must be met before handover. Handing over unprepared risks outages, keeping the project team indefinitely is not a transition, and closing anyway ignores the gap.

questions.stem: Two weeks ago, you escalated an impediment that is blocking your team, and it is still unresolved. What should you do?
options: Stop tracking it, since it has already been escalated to the right person
Ask the team to wait patiently and avoid mentioning it in stand-ups again
Follow up with the owner, reassess the impact and keep the status visible
Escalate it straight to the CEO, since the first escalation did not work
questions.explanation: Impediments are reassessed continually until they are removed, with follow-up on the owner and updated impact. Dropping it, silencing the team or jumping over the governance path are poor responses.

questions.stem: For each scope practice, select the approach it is most associated with.
rows: A scope baseline with a WBS and WBS dictionary
A product backlog ordered by the product owner
A change control board that approves scope changes
Scope refined each iteration based on feedback
Detailed scope defined before execution begins
questions.explanation: Predictive scope management defines scope up front, baselines it with a WBS and controls changes through a board. Adaptive scope management keeps an ordered backlog that is refined as feedback arrives each iteration.

questions.stem: Which TWO are appropriate estimating techniques for an agile team? (Choose two.)
options: Affinity estimating by relative size
Hours set by the project manager
Estimates copied from vendor quotes
Dates set from the sponsor's target
Planning poker with story points
questions.explanation: Agile teams estimate their own work with relative techniques such as planning poker and affinity grouping. Estimates imposed by a manager or sponsor, or copied from another source, are not team estimates and are less reliable.

questions.stem: A new tariff will raise the cost of imported components for your hybrid project by 20 percent from next quarter. What should you do?
options: Absorb the higher cost within the existing budget and say nothing about it to anyone
Buy all the components this week, before the tariff takes effect next quarter
Assess the impact on the budget and schedule and present options to the sponsor
Wait until the first invoice at the higher price arrives before taking action
questions.explanation: External changes are assessed for their impact and the options (for example, other suppliers, earlier purchase, a budget change) are put to the sponsor. Hiding the impact, making a large purchase without analysis or approval, or waiting all expose the project.

questions.stem: For each behavior, select the leadership style it shows.
rows: The leader clears blockers and protects the team's focus so members can deliver
The leader decides alone and then tells the team what will happen
The leader sets no direction and leaves the team to set its own goals
The leader asks questions that help a member find their own solution
questions.explanation: Servant leaders remove impediments and serve the team, directive leaders decide and instruct, laissez-faire leaders stay hands-off, and coaching leaders develop people by guiding them to their own answers.

questions.stem: A key business user has stopped attending sprint reviews, and recent increments have drifted from what her department needs. What should you do first?
options: Ask the team to build to the original requirements until she starts attending reviews again
Ask her manager to make attendance at every sprint review a part of her job objectives
Find out why she has stopped attending and adjust the review's timing or format if needed
Send her a recording of every review and ask her to send written feedback within two days
questions.explanation: Understanding why a stakeholder has disengaged comes first; the fix may be as simple as changing the time or making the review more relevant. Pressure through her manager, ignoring her needs or replacing discussion with recordings does not address the cause.

questions.stem: Your project will roll out a new point-of-sale system to 120 stores. Store layouts vary, and staff in a few stores have struggled with past system changes. Which execution strategy is best?
options: Install the system in the largest stores first, then decide whether to continue
Run a pilot in a few stores, apply what is learned, then roll out in waves
Switch all 120 stores to the new system on the same weekend to save time
Let each store manager decide when and how to install the new system
questions.explanation: A pilot followed by waves tests the solution in real conditions and lets lessons improve later waves, which suits varied sites and known adoption challenges. A big-bang cutover maximizes risk, uncoordinated rollout loses control, and starting with the largest stores puts the most revenue at risk first.

questions.stem: Your project's cost performance index has been about 0.85 for three months in a row. What should you do?
options: Ask for the cost baseline to be raised so that the index returns to 1.0
Wait one more month, since index values often recover on their own
Report the index to the sponsor as 1.0 until the trend can be explained
Identify the root cause of the overrun and propose corrective action
questions.explanation: A steady CPI below 1.0 is a trend, not noise; the project manager analyzes the cause and proposes corrective action through the proper channels. Waiting lets it grow, rebaselining to hide variance is inappropriate without an approved change, and misreporting is unethical.

questions.stem: A new AI service has become available that could automate a large part of the data-entry features on your backlog. What should you do?
options: Add the service to the product at once, since it will reduce the amount of work left in the backlog
Evaluate the service with the product owner, including its effect on the backlog, policy and risks
Ignore the service until the project is finished, since the backlog was agreed before it existed
Ask the team to replace the data-entry features with the service without telling the product owner
questions.explanation: Changes in technology are surveyed and assessed for their impact on scope and backlog, including organizational policy and new risks. The product owner decides on priorities. Adopting it blindly, ignoring it or acting without the product owner are all poor choices.

questions.stem: Customers keep finding defects after each release. The team says the test environment is to blame, while the testers say requirements are unclear. What should you do first?
options: Add a second round of manual testing at the end of every release to catch the defects
Buy a new test environment, since the team has identified it as the source of the problem
Ask the business analyst to rewrite every requirement in more detail before the next release
Lead the team through a root cause analysis of the escaped defects before choosing a fix
questions.explanation: With competing explanations, the next step is a structured root cause analysis using the defect data. Acting on one group's theory, whether new environments or rewritten requirements, may spend money on the wrong cause, and more end-of-line testing treats the symptom.

questions.stem: When should the lessons learned register be updated?
options: Only after an audit has identified a process problem
Only during project closure, once all of the work is accepted
Throughout the project, whenever a lesson is identified
Only at the end of each phase, during phase closure
questions.explanation: Lessons are captured as they arise so they can improve the current project as well as future ones. Waiting for phase or project closure loses detail and benefit, and audits are not the only source of lessons.

questions.stem: The sponsor has cancelled your project because of a change in company strategy. What should you do?
options: Keep working on the deliverables already in progress so that the effort is not wasted
Stop all work and release the team at once without recording where the project stands
Ask the sponsor to reconsider, and keep the whole team working while you wait for a final decision
Follow the closure process: record the status, release resources and capture lessons learned
questions.explanation: A cancelled project is still closed formally: document what was done and its status, settle contracts, release resources and capture lessons. Continuing work after cancellation wastes money, and walking away without records loses value for the organization.

questions.stem: How often does an agile team typically review its risks?
options: Only at the end of each release, as part of the release review
Once, at the start, when the team builds the full risk register
Only when the sponsor asks for a formal risk report on the work
Continually, in events like planning, stand-ups and retrospectives
questions.explanation: Agile teams handle risk continually through their regular events and by adding risk work to the backlog. One-time or occasional reviews miss risks that emerge between them.

questions.stem: Which TWO are components of the project management plan? (Choose two.)
options: The issue log with its current issues
The scope, schedule and cost baselines
Subsidiary plans such as risk and quality
The team's daily task board in its latest state
Raw work performance data from the team
questions.explanation: The project management plan holds the baselines and the subsidiary management plans. Issue logs, task boards and performance data are project documents or work outputs that the plan guides but does not contain.

questions.stem: When the cumulative planned cost of a project is plotted against time, what shape does the curve usually take?
options: A bell curve
An S-curve
A flat line
A straight drop
questions.explanation: Spending usually starts slowly, speeds up in execution and slows near the end, so the cumulative cost baseline forms an S-curve. Earned value and actual cost are plotted against it.

questions.stem: Your project is behind schedule. Before a board meeting, the sponsor asks you to report the status as green rather than amber. What should you do?
options: Report green this once, since the sponsor is accountable for the project
Ask a team member to present the status so you are not held responsible
Report green and add a note about the delay in the appendix of the report
Report the true status and explain your concerns to the sponsor
questions.explanation: Honesty in reporting is an ethical duty; the project manager reports the real status and discusses the concerns with the sponsor. Misreporting, burying the truth or passing the problem to someone else are all unethical.

questions.stem: A team member who is deaf has joined your team. Most team communication happens in voice calls. What should you do?
options: Ask a colleague to summarize each voice call for the new member in a short chat message after it ends
Assign the member work that needs the least discussion so meetings are less of a barrier
Ask the team member which accommodations work best for them and adjust meeting practices to match
Move all team communication to email so that every member receives information in the same way
questions.explanation: Supporting varied needs starts with asking the person, then adapting practices (for example live captions, chat alongside calls). Email-only slows the whole team, after-the-fact summaries exclude the person from discussion, and limiting their work is discriminatory.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project needs timely reviews from the IT security team before each release. That team does not report to you and has its own priorities. What is the best way to get its support?
options: Ask the sponsor to order the security team to make the project's reviews its top priority
Schedule the reviews in the project plan and then tell the security team when each one is due
Skip the reviews when the team is late and note them as an accepted risk in the register
Show how the project supports the security team's goals and agree a review process with them
questions.explanation: Influencing without authority works by building shared interest and agreeing a workable process. Using the sponsor's authority damages the relationship, scheduling others' work without agreement rarely works, and skipping required reviews creates compliance and security risk.

questions.stem: Your team must choose between two packaging designs. Design A costs less but creates more waste. Design B costs a little more and meets the company's published recycling target. What should you do?
options: Choose design B without consulting anyone, since sustainability always outweighs cost on every project
Leave the decision to the packaging supplier, since it knows the materials better than the project team
Choose design A, since the project's success is measured mainly by staying within the approved budget
Include the sustainability target in the quality requirements and evaluate both designs against them
questions.explanation: Quality requirements should capture stakeholder and organizational requirements such as sustainability targets, and options are evaluated against those agreed criteria. Choosing on cost alone or on sustainability alone without stakeholders, or handing the decision to a supplier, skips that step.

questions.stem: A problem that nobody had identified as a risk suddenly occurs, and the team responds on the spot. What is this unplanned response called?
options: A workaround
A fallback plan
A risk transfer
A contingency plan
questions.explanation: A workaround is an unplanned response to an unidentified risk or issue. Contingency and fallback plans are prepared in advance for identified risks, and transfer is a planned threat response.

questions.stem: A stakeholder insists that a data migration was always part of the project. The approved scope statement lists data migration as an exclusion. What should you do?
options: Show the stakeholder the approved exclusion and, if the need remains, raise a change request
Add the migration to the project plan, since the stakeholder is sure it was always intended
Ask the team to do the migration in their spare time so the scope baseline does not change
Refuse the stakeholder's request outright, since the scope statement has already been signed
questions.explanation: The approved scope statement settles what was agreed; if the stakeholder still needs the migration, change control evaluates it. Adding it without a decision causes scope creep, flatly refusing ignores a real need, and hidden work still costs time and money.

questions.stem: For four weeks in a row, a team lead has reported that a work package is 90 percent complete. What should you do?
options: Ask the team lead to report progress in hours spent instead of percent complete
Mark the work package as complete in the schedule so it stops delaying the report
Measure progress by finished deliverables that meet their acceptance criteria
Accept the reports, since the team lead knows the work better than anyone else
questions.explanation: Reported percent complete is subjective and often stalls near the end. Measuring progress by completed, accepted deliverables (or 0/100 rules for small packages) gives an honest status. Hours spent measure effort, not progress, and marking it complete misreports status.

questions.stem: The PMO's phase gate requires a complete requirements document before development can begin, but your team uses an agile approach. What should you do?
options: Skip the phase gate, since agile projects are not required to follow the organization's governance process
Switch the project to a predictive approach so that it fits the PMO's existing governance process exactly
Write a complete requirements document to pass the gate, then ignore it and work from the backlog anyway
Work with the PMO to tailor the gate criteria to evidence such as a refined backlog and working increments
questions.explanation: Governance can be tailored for agile work so it still gets the assurance it needs from different evidence. Producing a document only to ignore it wastes effort and misleads, skipping governance is not acceptable, and changing the delivery approach just to fit a gate ignores what the project needs.

questions.stem: In the daily stand-up, team members face you and report their progress to you rather than talking to each other. What should you do?
options: Replace the stand-up with a written status report that each team member sends to you every morning instead
Coach the team that the stand-up is for coordinating with each other, and step back from leading it
Keep running the stand-up, since team members are giving complete and useful status updates
Ask the product owner to run the stand-up instead so that updates focus on business priorities
questions.explanation: The stand-up is the team's planning and coordination event, not a status report to a manager. A servant leader coaches the team to own it. Keeping it as reporting, replacing it with written status or handing it to the product owner all miss its purpose.

questions.stem: Team members have heard rumors that the project will be cancelled, and morale is falling. What should you do?
options: Ask the team members to report whoever started the rumors so that it does not happen again
Confirm the facts with the sponsor, then share openly with the team what you can
Tell the team that the rumors are false, even though you are unsure whether that is true
Avoid the topic so that the rumors die down and the team stays focused on its work
questions.explanation: Transparency means finding out the facts and sharing them honestly. Denying something you cannot confirm risks trust, silence lets rumors grow, and hunting for the source creates fear.

questions.stem: A project has an earned value of \$70,000 and an actual cost of \$80,000. What is the cost variance? Type the number only, with no commas or currency sign, and use a minus sign if it is negative.
questions.explanation: CV = EV - AC = 70,000 - 80,000 = -10,000. A negative cost variance means the work done cost more than its planned value.

questions.stem: Two team members have had several sharp exchanges this week. You are not yet sure what the disagreement is about. What should you do first?
options: Ask the team to vote on which member's position is correct
Separate them by assigning them to different work packages
Talk with each of them to identify the source of the conflict
Tell them both that the next incident will be escalated to HR
questions.explanation: Conflict management starts with identifying its source and context. Separating people, issuing warnings or putting it to a vote all act before anyone knows what the conflict is about.

questions.stem: Which information belongs in the stakeholder register?
options: Each team member's hourly rate and weekly timesheet totals
The approved budget and its spending by month
Each stakeholder's interests, influence and expectations
The defects found in testing and who fixed them
questions.explanation: The stakeholder register records who the stakeholders are, their roles, interests, influence and expectations, and their classification. Rates, budgets and defects belong in other project documents.

questions.stem: On an agile team, who is accountable for maximizing the value of the product by ordering the product backlog?
options: The developers as a group
The team facilitator
The project sponsor
The product owner
questions.explanation: The product owner orders the backlog to maximize value, working with stakeholders and the team. The sponsor funds and champions the work, the facilitator supports the process, and the developers decide how to build the items.

questions.stem: How is a procurement contract formally closed?
options: The buyer gives the seller written notice that the contract is complete
The project manager deletes the contract from the procurement system
The project team stops contacting the seller once the work is delivered
The seller sends its final invoice and the buyer pays the amount on it
questions.explanation: Formal closure is usually a written notice from the buyer's authorized representative that the contract is complete, after deliverables are accepted and claims settled. Paying an invoice or ending contact does not formally close it.

questions.stem: What is the role of a change control board?
options: To review change requests and approve or reject them
To implement approved changes in the project deliverables
To write the change requests on behalf of stakeholders
To audit the project's quality processes once each quarter
questions.explanation: A change control board reviews, evaluates and approves, defers or rejects change requests. Stakeholders write requests, the team implements approved changes, and quality audits are a separate process.

questions.stem: Which information is typically recorded in a risk register?
options: Each stakeholder's contact details and preferred language
Each team member's working hours and vacation days
Each deliverable's acceptance date and sign-off record
Each risk's description, owner, rating and planned response
questions.explanation: The risk register lists identified risks with their causes, owners, probability and impact ratings, triggers and responses. Hours, contact details and sign-offs belong in other project records.

questions.stem: An activity has an early start of day 5 and a late start of day 9. How many days of total float does it have? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: Total float = late start - early start = 9 - 5 = 4 days (or late finish - early finish). The activity can slip up to 4 days without delaying the project.

questions.stem: Your new team has just come together. Members are polite but unsure of their roles and of what the project is trying to achieve. What should you focus on?
options: Setting strict performance targets so that members understand the standard expected of them
Clarifying the project's goals and each member's role, and helping members get to know each other
Letting members work out their own roles, since the team will settle into a pattern on its own
Assigning the hardest tasks first so that you can quickly identify the strongest performers on the team
questions.explanation: A team in the forming stage needs direction: clear goals, clear roles and a chance to build relationships. Leaving it to chance, setting strict targets or testing people with hard tasks does not address its uncertainty.

questions.stem: During a sprint review, a customer asks for several changes to the increment. What should happen to these requests?
options: The project manager rejects them because the sprint scope is already fixed
The team adds them to the current sprint so the customer sees them at once
The product owner adds them to the product backlog and prioritizes them
The customer submits a formal change request for the change control board
questions.explanation: In agile, new requests become backlog items that the product owner orders by value. Adding them mid-sprint breaks the sprint goal, rejecting feedback defeats the purpose of reviews, and a formal change board is not how an agile backlog changes.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the WBS dictionary?
options: To define the technical terms used in the project so that every stakeholder uses the same words
To show the order and dependencies of the activities needed to deliver each work package
To give the detail for each WBS component, such as its description, owner and acceptance criteria
To list the project's stakeholders with their roles, interests and level of influence on the work
questions.explanation: The WBS dictionary supports the WBS with detail for each component: description of work, responsible organization, milestones, acceptance criteria and estimates. A glossary defines terms, the stakeholder register lists stakeholders and the schedule network shows dependencies.

questions.stem: Which principle is central to modern quality management?
options: Prevention is better than inspection
Higher grade always means higher quality
Defects are best found by the customer
Quality is the inspector's job alone
questions.explanation: Building quality in through prevention costs less than finding defects later. Quality is everyone's responsibility, grade (features) differs from quality (fitness for use), and defects found by customers are the most expensive kind.

questions.stem: How does configuration management differ from change control?
options: Configuration management decides which change requests should be approved
Configuration management tracks the budget and schedule of each change request
Configuration management is used only on agile projects, not predictive ones
Configuration management controls the product's specifications and versions
questions.explanation: Configuration management identifies and controls the product's specifications, versions and documents; change control decides whether changes to the project and its baselines are approved. Both are used across approaches.

questions.stem: A threat has a 40 percent chance of causing a \$25,000 cost overrun. What is its expected monetary value? Type the number only, with no commas or currency sign, and use a minus sign for a cost.
questions.explanation: EMV = probability x impact = 0.40 x -25,000 = -10,000. Threat values are shown as negative because they reduce value.

questions.stem: A project has a budget at completion of \$250,000 and an estimate at completion of \$275,000. What is the variance at completion? Type the number only, with no commas or currency sign, and use a minus sign if it is negative.
questions.explanation: VAC = BAC - EAC = 250,000 - 275,000 = -25,000. The project is forecast to finish 25,000 over budget.

questions.stem: What is the main risk of fast tracking a schedule?
options: Lower quality, because testing is removed
Rework, because dependent activities overlap
A longer schedule, because work is spread out
Higher cost, because resources must be added
questions.explanation: Fast tracking runs activities in parallel that would normally be sequential, so later work may start on information that changes, causing rework. Added cost is the main trade-off of crashing, not fast tracking.

questions.stem: At sprint planning, the team asks you to assign the sprint's tasks to each person, as their previous manager did. What should you do?
options: Let the most senior developer assign the tasks so that the work is matched to members' skills
Ask the product owner to assign the tasks, since the product owner knows the priorities best
Encourage team members to choose their own tasks and coach them through the first few plans
Assign the tasks this time and plan to hand the job over once the team is more experienced
questions.explanation: Self-organizing teams decide among themselves who does what; the project manager coaches them into that habit. Assigning tasks, whether by the project manager, the product owner or a senior developer, keeps the old dependency in place.

questions.stem: In the sender-receiver model of communication, what confirms that a message was understood as intended?
options: Noise in the channel
Feedback from the receiver
Encoding by the sender
The medium used to send it
questions.explanation: Feedback (for example the receiver restating the message or asking questions) shows whether it was understood. The medium carries the message, encoding turns thoughts into a message, and noise interferes with it.

questions.stem: You are managing a small, low-risk internal project with a team of four. The PMO provides a full set of templates for large projects. What should you do?
options: Use every template in full, since the PMO provided them for all of the company's projects
Ask the PMO to write a new set of templates before the project is allowed to begin its work
Tailor the processes and documents to the project's size and risk, keeping what adds value
Skip planning documents entirely, since a small project does not need any formal planning
questions.explanation: Tailoring fits the approach and artifacts to the project's context, within governance requirements. Using everything wastes effort, skipping all planning invites problems, and waiting for new templates delays the work unnecessarily.

questions.stem: Which chart shows when a team member is over-allocated across the schedule?
options: A Pareto chart
A burndown chart
A resource histogram
A cause-and-effect diagram
questions.explanation: A resource histogram shows the hours scheduled for a resource in each period, so bars above the available limit show over-allocation. The other charts show defect causes, remaining sprint work and root causes.

questions.stem: A month after a new procurement system went live, many staff are still using their old spreadsheets instead. What should you do first?
options: Find out why staff are avoiding the system and address the barriers
Report the low use to senior managers and ask them to discipline staff
Ask IT to block the spreadsheets so staff have to use the new system
Close the project, since the system was delivered and formally accepted
questions.explanation: Adoption problems are understood before they are fixed; the barriers may be training, missing features or habits. Forcing use or discipline without understanding the cause breeds resistance, and benefits are not realized if people do not use the system.

questions.stem: How does an agile team usually handle the work needed to respond to an identified risk?
options: It leaves the risk work until all of the features have been delivered
It adds the risk work to the backlog and prioritizes it alongside features
It records the risk work in a register that only the sponsor can update
It hands the risk work to a separate team that runs outside the sprints
questions.explanation: A risk-adjusted backlog puts risk responses alongside features so the product owner orders them by value and risk. Separating the work, postponing it or restricting it to the sponsor delays the response.

questions.stem: On a cumulative flow diagram, the band for the testing column keeps getting wider while the band for done stays thin. What does this suggest?
options: Testing is the fastest stage in the team's workflow
The team has too few items waiting in its backlog
Work is piling up in testing, which is a bottleneck
The team is finishing work faster than it starts it
questions.explanation: A widening band means items are entering a stage faster than they leave it: a bottleneck. The team should look at limiting work in progress and helping the testing stage, as a thin done band shows little is being finished.

questions.stem: Which TWO behaviors are signs of a high-performing team? (Choose two.)
options: Members avoid disagreeing with each other to keep the atmosphere positive
Members raise concerns openly and early, even when they are uncomfortable
Work is always assigned according to each member's seniority
Members hold each other accountable for agreed commitments
The project manager approves every technical decision before work begins
questions.explanation: High-performing teams share accountability and are safe enough to raise problems early. Central approval of every decision, avoiding healthy conflict and seniority-based assignment are signs of a team that is not yet performing.

questions.stem: On a hybrid project, which TWO actions best keep business stakeholders engaged? (Choose two.)
options: Send them the full backlog each week without a summary
Invite them to sprint reviews to see working increments
Ask team members to email stakeholders on their own
Share a milestone roadmap that shows the coming releases
Limit contact with them to the end of each project phase
questions.explanation: Seeing working results and a clear roadmap keeps stakeholders involved and lets them steer. Raw backlog dumps overwhelm, phase-end-only contact misses chances to give feedback, and uncoordinated emails create confusion.

questions.stem: A product owner sorts backlog items into must have, should have, could have and will not have this time. Which technique is this?
options: Monte Carlo simulation
MoSCoW prioritization
Pareto analysis
Kano analysis
questions.explanation: MoSCoW groups requirements into must, should, could and will not have. The Kano model classifies features by how they affect satisfaction, Pareto analysis finds the few causes behind most problems, and Monte Carlo simulation models schedule or cost uncertainty.

questions.stem: What is test-driven development?
options: Having a separate team test the code after each sprint ends
Testing the whole product once at the end of each release
Driving the release date from the number of tests that have passed
Writing an automated test before the code that makes it pass
questions.explanation: In test-driven development a developer writes a failing test, then the code to pass it, then refactors. It builds quality in continuously instead of testing at the end or handing testing to another team.

questions.stem: A team reviews political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors that could affect its project. Which analysis is this?
options: Earned value analysis
Root cause analysis
SWOT analysis
PESTLE analysis
questions.explanation: PESTLE analysis scans the external environment across those six areas. SWOT covers strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, root cause analysis looks for the causes of a problem, and earned value analysis measures performance.

questions.stem: Which technique runs many simulated iterations of the schedule, using ranges of activity durations, to estimate the probability of meeting a finish date?
options: Expert judgment
Monte Carlo simulation
Decision tree analysis
Critical path method
questions.explanation: Monte Carlo simulation samples from duration (or cost) ranges thousands of times to produce a probability distribution of outcomes. The critical path method gives a single finish date, expert judgment is not a simulation, and decision trees compare choices by expected value.

questions.stem: What is the duration of a milestone in a project schedule?
options: One week
Its float
Zero
One day
questions.explanation: A milestone marks a significant point or event, such as approval of a deliverable, and has zero duration. It is not an activity with work or time attached.
